rpc_codal.article_title: Substituting and altering trade-marks and trade-names
rpc_codal.content_md:
The penalty of prision correccional in its minimum period or a fine ranging from 200 to 1,000 pesos or both, shall be imposed upon:

1. Any person who shall substitute the name or mark of some other manufacturer for the name or mark of the real manufacturer upon any article of commerce and shall sell the same;

2. Any person who shall sell such articles of commerce or offer the same for sale, knowing that the trade-mark has been fraudulently used in such goods as described in the preceding subdivision; or

3. Any person who, knowing the purposes for which the trade-mark or trade-name of a person is to be used, prints, lithographs, or in any way reproduces such trade-mark or trade-name, or a colorable imitation thereof, for another person, to enable that other person to fraudulently use such trade-mark or trade-name on his own goods.

A trade-name or trade-mark is a word or words, name, emblem, sign, or device used as an advertisement, sign, label, poster or otherwise, for the purpose of enabling the public to distinguish the business of the person who owns and uses said trade-name or trade-mark.
rpc_codal.section_label: Frauds in commerce and industry

rpc_codal.title_label:
TITLE FOUR
CRIMES AGAINST PUBLIC INTEREST
rpc_codal.content_md:
A youthful offender is a child, minor or youth, including one who is emancipated in accordance with law who is over nine years but under eighteen years of age at the time of the commission of the offense.

A Child nine years of age or under at the time of the commission of the offense shall be exempt from criminal liability and shall be committed to the care of his or her father or mother, or nearest relative or family friend in the discretion of the court and subject to its supervision. The same shall be done for a child over nine years and under fifteen years of age at the time of the commission of the offense, unless he acted with discernment, in which case he shall be proceeded against in accordance with Article 192.

The provisions of Article 80 of the Revised Penal Code are hereby repealed by the provisions of this Chapter.

amendments.description:
**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Formal Revision

*(This is categorized as a "Formal Revision" not because it revises the text of RPC Article 189, but because the provided data presents a formal error of attribution. The analysis will clarify that the "New Amendment" does not actually amend the subject article of the Revised Penal Code.)*

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
The provided text from Presidential Decree No. 1179 does not amend, modify, or in any way affect Article 189 of the Revised Penal Code, which deals with Unfair Competition. Instead, P.D. 1179 amends Article 189 of a completely different statute: Presidential Decree No. 603, otherwise known as "The Child and Youth Welfare Code." The "New Amendment" redefines a youthful offender by lowering the maximum age from twenty-one (under P.D. 603) to eighteen.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
- **Elements of the Crime**: There is **no change** to the elements of Unfair Competition or Fraudulent Registration of Trademark under RPC Article 189. The "New Amendment" is entirely unrelated to this substantive crime.

- **Penalty Shift**: There is **no shift** in the penalties for violations of RPC Article 189. The penalties of *prision correccional* in its minimum period or a fine remain unchanged by this decree.

- **"Ghost" Law Effect**: While P.D. 1179 is presented as an amendment to Article 189, its true impact on the Revised Penal Code is that of a "ghost" law affecting a different article entirely. The last paragraph of the new text explicitly states, "The provisions of Article 80 of the Revised Penal Code are hereby repealed..." Therefore, the operational impact of P.D. 1179 was to formally repeal the RPC's original provision on youthful offenders (Art. 80) and replace it with the new framework established under the Child and Youth Welfare Code. It had no effect on RPC Article 189.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
The juxtaposition of these two texts highlights a common point of confusion arising from identically numbered articles across different statutes. The "Previous Text" is the original formulation of Article 189 of the Revised Penal Code of 1930, a crime against public interest involving intellectual property.

The "New Amendment," P.D. 1179, belongs to a separate legal lineage concerning juvenile justice. This lineage began with Article 80 of the Revised Penal Code itself. This was later superseded by a more comprehensive special law, P.D. 603 ("The Child and Youth Welfare Code"), which contained its own "Article 189" defining youthful offenders. P.D. 1179 then amended *that* specific article in P.D. 603.

In summary, there is no direct evolutionary relationship between the "Previous Text" and the "New Amendment." The law on Unfair Competition under RPC Article 189 was left untouched by the developments in juvenile justice law. The new text's only relevance to the RPC was its express repeal of Article 80, not its non-existent amendment of Article 189.

rpc_codal.title_label:
TITLE TWO
PERSONS CRIMINALLY LIABLE FOR FELONIES
rpc_codal.content_md:
Accessories are those who, having knowledge of the commission of the crime, and without having participated therein, either as principals or accomplices, take part subsequent to its commission in any of the following manners:

1. By profiting themselves or assisting the offenders to profit by the effects of the crime.

2. By concealing or destroying the body of the crime, or the effects or instruments thereof, in order to prevent its discovery.

3. By harboring, concealing, or assisting in the escape of the principal of the crime, provided the accessory acts with abuse of his public functions or Whenever the author of the crime is guilty of treason, parricide, murder, or an attempt to take the life of the Chief Executive, or is known to be habitually guilty of some other crime.

GENERAL PROVISIONS REGARDING THE DATE OF ENFORCEMENT AND APPLICATION OF THE PROVISIONS OF THIS CODE, AND REGARDING THE OFFENSES, THE PERSONS LIABLE AND THE PENALTIES

rpc_codal.title_label:
TITLE FIVE
CRIMES RELATIVE TO OPIUM AND OTHER PROHIBITED DRUGS
rpc_codal.content_md:
It shall be the duty of the law-enforcement agency concerned to take the youthful offender, after his apprehension, to any available government medical or health officer in the area for a physical and mental examination. Whenever treatment for any physical or mental defect is indicated, steps shall be immediately undertaken to provide the same.

The examination and treatment papers shall form part of the record of the case of the youthful offender.

amendments.description:
**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Decriminalization

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
Presidential Decree No. 1179 completely replaces the text of Article 190. The original article, which penalized the possession and use of prohibited drugs and the maintenance of drug dens, has been entirely removed. In its place, a new procedural rule is established, mandating the physical and mental examination of apprehended youthful offenders by government health officers.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
- **Elements of the Crime**: The crime of possession of prohibited drugs under Article 190 is effectively repealed from the Revised Penal Code. Consequently, all its elements cease to exist within the RPC framework. The new text does not define a crime but instead imposes a procedural duty on law enforcement, and as such, it contains no elements for a criminal offense.

- **Penalty Shift**: The penalty of *arresto mayor* in its medium period to *prision correccional* in its minimum period and a fine is completely eliminated from this article. The new provision is administrative and carries no direct penal sanction itself.

- **Operational Impact of "Ghost" Law**: This amendment is a direct consequence of a "ghost" law, Republic Act No. 6425 (The Dangerous Drugs Act of 1972). RA 6425 created a comprehensive special penal law that superseded the RPC's provisions on drug offenses. PD 1179 acts as a "clean-up" amendment, formally removing the now-redundant drug-related text from the RPC and repurposing the article number. All prosecutions for acts formerly covered by the original Article 190 would henceforth be exclusively governed by the special law (RA 6425 and its successors), which provides for different penalties, prescription periods, and bail rules.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
The original Article 190 was the RPC's primary tool against drug offenses. However, the enactment of RA 6425 in 1972 consolidated all drug-related legislation into a single, specialized statute, rendering Article 190 obsolete.

Presidential Decree No. 1179, issued in 1977, formally acknowledges this legislative shift by excising the now-superseded provision from the Code. Instead of leaving the article number blank, the legislative authority repurposed it to insert a provision related to another area of legal development at the time: juvenile justice. The new text is thematically aligned with Presidential Decree No. 603 (The Child and Youth Welfare Code), reflecting a new focus on the proper handling and rehabilitation of youthful offenders. This change illustrates a common legislative practice where an article, having lost its original purpose due to being absorbed by a special law, is repurposed to house a new, unrelated legal concept.

rpc_codal.article_title: Keeper, watchman and visitor of opium den
rpc_codal.content_md:

1. Anyone who shall act as keeper or watchman of a dive or resort where any prohibited drug is used in any manner contrary to law; and

rpc_codal.article_title: Suspension Of Sentence And Commitment Of Youthful Offender
rpc_codal.content_md:
If after hearing the evidence in the proper proceedings, the court should find that the youthful offender has committed the acts charged against him, the court shall determine the imposable penalty, including any civil liability chargeable against him. ### **ANALYSIS OF AMENDMENT TO REVISED PENAL CODE ARTICLE 192**

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Formal Revision

*(Note: This represents a complete repeal and subject matter replacement, not a modification of the original crime. The offense under the original Art. 192 was repealed and transferred to a special penal law, and a new legal concept concerning juvenile justice was subsequently introduced.)*

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
This amendment does not modify the original Article 192 but rather reflects its total repeal and the introduction of an entirely new legal principle. The original article, which penalized the importation and sale of prohibited drugs, was rendered obsolete and expressly repealed by subsequent special legislation. The concept introduced by Presidential Decree No. 1179, suspension of sentence for youthful offenders, represents a fundamental shift in legal philosophy concerning juvenile justice, replacing the former subject matter of the article entirely.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
-   **Elements of the Crime**: The original crime defined in Article 192 ceased to exist within the Revised Penal Code. Its elements and the prosecution of drug-related offenses were transferred to and are now governed by a special penal law, The Dangerous Drugs Act of 1972 (Republic Act No. 6425), and its subsequent iterations. The new concept introduced by P.D. 1179 does not define a crime but establishes a special procedural and dispositional rule for minors in conflict with the law.

-   **Penalty Shift**: The penalty of `prision correccional` for drug importation and sale under the old Art. 192 became inapplicable. R.A. 6425 established a new, more complex, and generally harsher penalty structure for drug offenses. The "amendment" itself does not impose a penalty; instead, it creates an alternative to the imposition of a penalty and judgment of conviction for a specific class of offenders (youthful offenders), allowing for their commitment and rehabilitation instead of penal servitude.

-   **"Ghost Law" Impact**: This is a classic example of a change effected by a "ghost law." Republic Act No. 6425 is the primary "ghost law" that operated on the original Article 192. Section 39 of R.A. 6425 expressly repealed Articles 190, 191, 192, 193, and 194 of the Revised Penal Code. This action removed the subject matter of prohibited drugs from the RPC, even though the physical text might have remained in older prints of the Code, functionally rendering it a dead letter.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
The evolution of this article is not a linear amendment but a tale of legislative substitution and philosophical change.

Initially, the Revised Penal Code of 1932 provided a general penalty for drug offenses under Articles 190-194. However, as the drug problem became more complex, the legislature opted for a comprehensive and specialized legal framework. This culminated in the passage of the Dangerous Drugs Act of 1972 (R.A. 6425), which provided a detailed and more severe regime for drug crimes and expressly repealed the corresponding RPC provisions.

Concurrently, a separate evolution was occurring in jurisprudence regarding juvenile justice. The purely punitive model was being replaced by a rehabilitative one. This was first institutionalized in Presidential Decree No. 603 (The Child and Youth Welfare Code) in 1974, which introduced the suspension of sentence for youthful offenders. Presidential Decree No. 1179 in 1977 further amended and refined this procedure.

Therefore, the "change" to Article 192 is a two-fold historical event:
1.  The subject of drug offenses was completely carved out of the RPC and transferred to a special law (R.A. 6425), making the original Article 192 obsolete.
2.  The legal system simultaneously developed a new framework for juvenile justice (P.D. 603, as amended by P.D. 1179), introducing the concept of suspended sentences. While this new concept was not directly inserted into the now-vacant Article 192 of the RPC at that exact moment, it represents the new legal doctrine that supplanted the old punitive model, especially for minors. This rehabilitative approach would later be strengthened and institutionalized by R.A. 9344 (The Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006).

### **ANALYSIS OF AMENDMENT TO REVISED PENAL CODE ARTICLE 193**

---

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Formal Revision

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
Presidential Decree No. 1179 completely repeals the original Article 193, which defined and penalized the crime of illegal possession of drug paraphernalia. The decree replaces it with an entirely new provision of a procedural nature, which makes an order denying an application for suspension of sentence non-appealable.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
*   **Elements of the Crime**: The amendment effectively removes the crime of "Illegal possession of an opium pipe or other paraphernalia" from this specific article of the Revised Penal Code. Consequently, the elements of said crime are no longer found here. This act is now governed and prosecuted under a special penal law, the Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act (currently R.A. 9165, which superseded earlier drug laws). The `prima facie` evidence rule contained in the original article is also rendered inoperative within the RPC.

*   **Penalty Shift**: The penalty of `arresto mayor` and a fine not exceeding 500 pesos is entirely eliminated from this article, as the underlying crime has been removed. The new provision does not impose a penalty but establishes a procedural limitation on the right to appeal.

*   **Procedural Impact**: The new Article 193 introduces a rule on remedial law. It explicitly bars an appeal from an order denying an application for suspension of sentence. This is consistent with the general principle that interlocutory orders are not appealable until after a final judgment on the merits is rendered, thereby preventing undue delay and piecemeal appeals.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
This amendment exemplifies how special penal laws supersede provisions of the Revised Penal Code. The original Article 193 became obsolete following the enactment of more comprehensive legislation specifically targeting drug offenses, most notably Republic Act No. 6425 (The Dangerous Drugs Act of 1972).

P.D. 1179, enacted in 1977, served as an administrative "clean-up" of the RPC. Recognizing that the subject matter of the old Article 193 was already absorbed and more extensively covered by the Dangerous Drugs Act, the legislator repurposed the article number. Instead of leaving it as a dead-letter provision, it was replaced with a new rule of procedure that is logically connected to the provisions on youthful offenders in the immediately preceding Article 192. This is not a decriminalization of the act itself, but rather a legislative migration of the offense from the general code (RPC) to a specialized statute, with the now-vacant article number being recycled for a new, unrelated purpose.

### **Analysis of Article 195 of the Revised Penal Code as amended by Commonwealth Act No. 235**

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Penalty Upgrade

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
Commonwealth Act No. 235 substantially restructures Article 195 by stratifying the penalties for illegal gambling. It segregates the maintainers, conductors, or bankers of the game of "jueteng" from other gambling participants. This amendment imposes a significantly higher penalty on this specific group, while retaining the original, lighter penalty for ordinary bettors and other minor participants.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
- **Elements of the Crime**: While the actus reus (the prohibited gambling activities) remains unchanged, this amendment effectively creates a qualified version of the offense. To secure a conviction under the new, harsher provision, the prosecution must now prove not only the existence of the illegal game of *jueteng* but also that the accused's specific role was that of a "maintainer, conductor, or banker." The offender's level of participation is now a material element determining the imposable penalty.

- **Penalty Shift**:
    - For **maintainers, conductors, or bankers of *jueteng***, the penalty is drastically elevated from what was previously a light felony (`arresto mayor` for recidivists, 1 month and 1 day to 6 months) to a less grave felony: `prision correccional` in its maximum degree (4 years, 2 months, and 1 day to 6 years).
    - For **all other participants** (e.g., bettors or those involved in games other than *jueteng*), the original light penalty of `arresto menor` (1 to 30 days) remains.
    - This upgrade to a correctional penalty also carries with it more severe accessory penalties, including suspension from public office and the right of suffrage, and civil interdiction for the duration of the sentence.

- **Prescription of Crimes**: The penalty shift has a direct and significant consequence on the prescriptive period of the offense.
    - The original offense, being a light felony, would prescribe in one (1) year.
    - The new, qualified offense for *jueteng* maintainers, being a less grave felony punishable by a correctional penalty, now prescribes in ten (10) years, pursuant to Article 90 of the RPC. This gives the State a much longer period to prosecute the masterminds of such operations.

- **Bail Eligibility**: While the offense remains bailable, the classification as a less grave felony with a potential sentence of up to six years would substantively increase the recommended amount of bail compared to that for a light felony.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
The original text of Article 195 in the 1930 Revised Penal Code applied a uniform, and relatively light, penalty to all persons involved in illegal gambling, making little distinction between a high-level operator and a common bettor. This approach proved insufficient in curbing organized gambling operations.

Commonwealth Act No. 235 represents a critical shift in legislative policy. The amendment acknowledges the different levels of culpability and social harm posed by different actors in the illegal gambling hierarchy. By isolating the "maintainer, conductor, or banker" of *jueteng*—a notoriously widespread and organized numbers game in the Philippines—and imposing a significantly heavier penalty, the law aims to dismantle the organizational and financial backbone of these illegal enterprises. This change reflects a more sophisticated legislative intent to target the source and management of the illegal activity, rather than merely punishing the end-users or minor participants.

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Decriminalization

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
This amendment does not modify the original Article 195 but completely replaces it with an entirely new and unrelated provision. The original article, which defined and penalized illegal gambling, has been removed. The new text under the same article number establishes a procedural requirement for reporting on the progress of a youthful offender under the care of the state.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
- **Elements of the Crime**: The amendment effectively expunges the crime of gambling, as defined in the original Article 195, from the Revised Penal Code. Consequently, all elements related to participating in, maintaining, or permitting illegal games of chance under this specific article are rendered obsolete. The new text does not define a crime but instead imposes an administrative duty on social welfare entities.

- **Penalty Shift**: All penalties associated with the original article—ranging from *arresto menor* to *prision correccional*—are removed. The new text contains no penal sanction; it is a directive concerning the supervision of youthful offenders.

- **Operational Impact of Superseding Law**: In practice, this change reflects the express repeal of Articles 195-199 of the Revised Penal Code by **Presidential Decree No. 1602** ("Simplifying and Providing for Stiffer Penalties for Illegal Gambling"). P.D. 1602, a special penal law, now governs the crime of illegal gambling, imposing significantly higher penalties than the original RPC provision. Therefore, while Article 195 is now a "dead-letter" provision in the RPC concerning gambling, the act itself was not decriminalized but is now prosecuted under a different, more stringent law. The text provided in the "New Amendment" appears to be incorrectly attributed, as it mirrors Article 195 of P.D. 603 (The Child and Youth Welfare Code), not a direct amendment to the RPC.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
The original Article 195 of the 1930 Revised Penal Code represented the state's foundational policy against various forms of illegal gambling. However, by the 1970s, the penalties were considered too light to be an effective deterrent against the proliferation of organized and large-scale gambling operations like *jueteng*.

The "amendment" signifies a complete legislative overhaul rather than an incremental change. The Marcos administration opted to address the inadequacy of the RPC provisions not by amending them, but by creating a comprehensive special penal law, P.D. 1602, in 1978. This decree consolidated all gambling laws and imposed much stiffer penalties, such as *prision correccional* in its medium period as a minimum penalty for bettors. This act repealed the RPC's gambling provisions, including Article 195, by specific provision. The result is that gambling is no longer prosecuted under the Revised Penal Code but under this special law, which has since been further amended by R.A. 9287 to impose even harsher penalties for *jueteng* and other number games.

TITLE SIX
CRIMES AGAINST PUBLIC MORALS
rpc_codal.article_title: What Acts Are Punishable In Gambling.
rpc_codal.content_md:
(a) The penalty of arresto menor or a fine not exceeding two hundred pesos, and, in case of recidivism, the penalty of arresto mayor or a fine ranging from two hundred to six thousand pesos, shall be imposed upon:

1. Any person other than those referred to in subsections (b) and (c) who, in any manner, shall directly or indirectly take part in any game of 'monte,' 'jueteng' or any other form of lottery, policy, banking or percentage game, dog races or any other game or scheme the result of which depends wholly or chiefly upon chance or hazard; or wherein wagers consisting of money, articles of value or representative of value are made; or in the exploitation or use of any other mechanical invention or contrivance to determine by chance the loser or winner of money or any object or representative of value.

2. Any person who shall knowingly permit any form of gambling referred to in the preceding subdivision to be carried on in any inhabited or uninhabited place or any building, vessel or other means of transportation owned or controlled by him. If the place where gambling is carried on has the reputation of a gambling place or that prohibited gambling is frequently carried on therein, the culprit shall be punished by the penalty provided for in this article in its maximum period.

(b) The penalty of prision correctional in its maximum degree shall be imposed upon the maintainer, conductor, or banker in a game of 'jueteng' or any similar game.

(c) The penalty of prision correctional in its medium degree shall be imposed upon any person who shall, knowingly and without lawful purpose, have in his possession any lottery list, paper or other matter containing letters, figures, signs or symbols which pertain to or are in any manner used in the game of 'jueteng' or any similar game which has taken place or about to take place.

TITLE SIX
CRIMES AGAINST PUBLIC MORALS
rpc_codal.article_title: Importation, sale and possession of lottery tickets or advertisements
rpc_codal.content_md:
The penalty of arresto mayor in its maximum period to prision correccional in its minimum period or a fine ranging from 200 to 2,000 pesos, or both, in the discretion of the court, shall be imposed upon any person who shall import into the Philippine Islands from any foreign place or port any lottery ticket or advertisement or, in connivance with the importer, shall sell or distribute the same.

Any person who shall knowingly and with intent to use them, have in his possession lottery tickets or advertisements, or shall sell or distribute the same without connivance with the importer of the same, shall be punished by arresto menor, or a fine not exceeding 200 pesos, or both, in the discretion of the court.

The possession of any lottery ticket or advertisement shall be prima facie evidence of an intent to sell, distribute or use the same in the Philippine Islands.

rpc_codal.article_title: Return Of The Youthful Offender To Court.
rpc_codal.content_md:
Whenever the youthful offender has been found incorrigible or has willfully failed to comply with the conditions of his rehabilitation programs, or should his continued stay in the training institution be inadvisable, he shall be returned to the committing court for the pronouncement of judgment.

When the youthful offender has reached the age of twenty-one while in commitment, the court shall determine whether to dismiss the case in accordance with the extent preceding article or to pronounce the judgment conviction. In the latter case, the convicted offender may apply for probation under the provisions of Presidential Decree Numbered Nine Hundred and Sixty-Eight.

In any case covered by this article, the youthful offender shall be credited in the service of his sentence with the full time spent in actual commitment and detention effected under the provisions of this Chapter.

amendments.description:
### 1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY
Formal Revision

### 2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE
This amendment does not modify the original Article 197 but instead completely repeals and replaces it. The article's subject matter is entirely changed from the crime of betting on sports contests to a procedural rule concerning the return of a youthful offender to the committing court. Presidential Decree No. 1179 effectively removed the old provision and inserted a new one with a different title and substance.

### 3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT
-   **Elements of the Crime**: The original crime of "Betting in sports contests," as defined in the previous version of Article 197, is effectively repealed from the Revised Penal Code by this amendment. The new Article 197 does not define a crime or its elements; instead, it establishes a procedural framework for handling youthful offenders who fail rehabilitation or reach the age of majority while under commitment.

-   **Penalty Shift**: There is no penalty shift for the original crime, as the crime itself has been removed from this article. The new provision does not impose a penalty but rather dictates the procedure for the pronouncement of judgment for the original offense committed by the youthful offender. It introduces significant new concepts, such as the option to apply for probation under P.D. 968 and the mandatory crediting of time spent in detention and commitment against the eventual sentence.

-   **Substantive Impact**: The amendment introduces a special procedural rule into the Revised Penal Code, integrating concepts from the Child and Youth Welfare Code (P.D. 603, which P.D. 1179 amends). It creates a distinct pathway for youthful offenders, allowing for judicial discretion to either dismiss the case or pronounce judgment upon the offender reaching the age of twenty-one. The provision granting credit for time served in a training institution is a significant substantive right granted to the youthful offender.

### 4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP
This amendment represents a complete thematic and substantive overhaul of Article 197, reflecting a major legislative initiative during the 1970s to establish a distinct juvenile justice system.

The previous article was a remnant of the original 1930 RPC, criminalizing a specific light felony related to gambling. The new amendment, P.D. 1179, was part of a series of decrees building the framework of the Child and Youth Welfare Code. The legislative choice was not to simply amend the original gambling provision but to repurpose the article number entirely for this new framework.

This change signals a legislative priority shift from punishing minor vices to creating specialized procedures for juvenile delinquents. The repeal of the old article on sports betting and its replacement with a procedural rule on youthful offenders demonstrates the practice of using available or low-impact RPC article numbers as vessels for introducing significant, and often thematically unrelated, legal reforms from other special laws. The original crime was effectively decriminalized *within the RPC*, and the article number was repurposed to serve the aims of the then-nascent juvenile justice and welfare system.

rpc_codal.title_label:
TITLE SIX
CRIMES AGAINST PUBLIC MORALS
rpc_codal.content_md:
The penalty of arresto menor or a fine not exceeding 200 pesos, or both, shall be imposed upon any person who, except during the periods allowed by law, shall bet on horse races. The penalty of arresto mayor or a fine ranging from 200 to 2,000 pesos, or both, shall be imposed upon any person who, under the same circumstances, shall maintain or employ a totalizer or other device or scheme for betting on horse races or realizing any profit therefrom.

For the purposes of this article, any race held on the same day and at the same place shall be held punishable as a separate offense, and if the same be committed by any partnership, corporation or association, the president and the directors or managers thereof shall be deemed to be principals in the offense if they have consented to or knowingly tolerated its commission.

rpc_codal.title_label:
TITLE SIX
CRIMES AGAINST PUBLIC MORALS
rpc_codal.content_md:
The penalty of arresto menor or a fine not exceeding 200 pesos, or both, in the discretion of the court, shall be imposed upon:

1. Any person who directly or indirectly participates in cockfights, by betting money or other valuable things, or who organizes cockfights at which bets are made, on a day other than those permitted by law.

2. Any person who directly or indirectly participates in cockfights, by betting money or other valuable things, or organizes such cockfights, at a place other than a licensed cockpit.

rpc_codal.title_label:
PRELIMINARY TITLE
DATE OF EFFECTIVENESS AND APPLICATION OF THE PROVISIONS OF THIS CODE
rpc_codal.content_md:
Except as provided in the treaties and laws of preferential application, the provisions of this Code shall be enforced not only within the Philippine Archipelago, including its atmosphere, its interior waters and maritime zone, but also outside of its jurisdiction, against those who:

1. Should commit an offense while on a Philippine ship or airship.

2. Should forge or counterfeit any coin or currency note of the Philippine Islands or obligations and securities issued by the Government of the Philippine Islands.

3. Should be liable for acts connected with the introduction into these Islands of the obligations and securities mentioned in the preceding number.

4. While being public officers or employees, should commit an offense in the exercise of their functions; or

5. Should commit any of the crimes against national security and the law of nations, defined in *Title* One of Book Two of this Code.

amendments.description:
### 1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY
**Formal Revision**

### 2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE
The text provided under Republic Act No. 7659 is an exact reproduction of the original Article 2 of the Revised Penal Code. There are no literal alterations, additions, or deletions to the substantive provisions governing the extraterritorial application of the Code. The five circumstances under which the RPC applies outside the Philippines remain identical.

### 3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT
This is a classic example of a "Ghost" amendment, where the cited law (RA 7659) does not alter the text of the article itself but has a profound operational impact on its application.

-   **Elements of the Crime:** There is no change to the elements of any crime. Article 2 is a rule on jurisdiction and does not define criminal offenses. The five enumerated grounds for extraterritorial jurisdiction are untouched.

-   **Penalty Shift:** While Article 2 itself prescribes no penalty, its function is to establish jurisdiction over offenses committed abroad. RA 7659, the Heinous Crimes Act of 1993, significantly increased the penalties for various crimes, including re-imposing the death penalty. Therefore, while the text of Article 2 remains the same, the *consequences* for committing an offense covered by its extraterritorial scope were drastically heightened. For instance, if a public officer committed a grave offense in the exercise of their functions abroad (paragraph 4) or a person committed a crime against national security like treason (paragraph 5), the imposable penalty for the underlying crime would now be subject to the harsher penalties mandated by RA 7659, potentially including death.

-   **Prescription of Crimes / Bail Eligibility:** The impact is indirect. By increasing the penalties for the underlying crimes to death (at the time), RA 7659 rendered those offenses non-bailable as a matter of right. Similarly, the prescription periods for crimes and their penalties are tied to the severity of the penalty; increasing the penalty could lengthen the prescriptive period for the offense.

### 4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP
The amendment history here is not one of direct textual change but of substantive consequence. RA 7659 was enacted in response to a public clamor against a perceived rise in heinous criminality, with the legislative intent of imposing a strong deterrent through more severe punishments.

Article 2 was not the target of the amendment; rather, it served as a jurisdictional predicate for the newly enhanced penalties. The "Why" is the legislative policy to deter heinous crimes, regardless of where they are committed, as long as Philippine courts could exercise jurisdiction under the established principles of extraterritoriality. The "How" is the operational effect: the law did not need to change the jurisdictional rule of Article 2, but by changing the penalties for the crimes themselves, it fundamentally altered the gravity and legal ramifications for any person who might commit such an act outside the Philippines but still fall under its legal purview.

In essence, RA 7659 did not revise the *reach* of Philippine criminal law as defined in Article 2, but it significantly increased the *force of its blow* when that reach was established.

rpc_codal.article_title: Accessories Who Are Exempt From Criminal Liability.
rpc_codal.content_md: The penalties prescribed for accessories shall not be imposed upon those who are such with respect to their spouses, ascendants, descendants, legitimate, natural, and adopted brothers and sisters, or relatives by affinity within the same degrees, with the single exception of accessories falling within the provisions of paragraph 1 of the next preceding article.

amendments.description:
### **ANALYSIS OF ARTICLE 20 OF THE REVISED PENAL CODE**

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Formal Revision

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
Republic Act No. 7659 did not introduce any substantive change to this article. The amendment is purely formal, re-stating the original text of the law verbatim while officially incorporating the article number and title ("Article 20. Accessories who are exempt from criminal liability.") into the statutory text as part of a larger legislative enactment.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
- **Elements of the Crime**: This amendment has no effect on the elements of any crime. Article 20 does not define a crime but rather provides a personal ground for exemption from criminal liability for the felony of being an accessory. The conditions for this exemption—relationship to the principal offender and the exception under Article 19, Paragraph 1—remain completely unchanged.

- **Penalty Shift**: There is no penalty shift. The core function of the article is to exempt certain individuals from the imposition of penalties, and this function was not modified.

- **Prescription of Crimes / Bail Eligibility**: This formal revision has no impact on the prescription of crimes or bail eligibility, as it did not alter any substantive provision, penalty, or classification of an offense.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
This amendment presents a common legislative phenomenon where an article is re-published without substantive change within a larger amending law. Republic Act No. 7659, known as the Heinous Crimes Act of 1993, was primarily enacted to re-impose the death penalty and increase penalties for a range of serious offenses.

The inclusion of Article 20 in RA 7659 was not intended to alter the long-standing rule on accessory liability exemptions for relatives. It was likely re-enacted for completeness or as a structural consequence of amendments to other related articles within the Revised Penal Code. For the legal scholar or bar candidate, the critical takeaway is that despite being mentioned in a law famed for escalating penalties, Article 20 itself was merely carried over. The underlying legal principle, which grants immunity to individuals who act as accessories to protect their close relatives (except when they profit from the crime or harbor the principal), remains a steadfast and unaltered doctrine from the original text of the Code.

amendments.description:
## ANALYSIS OF AMENDMENT TO ARTICLE 201 OF THE REVISED PENAL CODE

### 1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY
Fine Escalation | Penalty Upgrade | Element Modification

### 2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE
Republic Act No. 10951 significantly escalates the pecuniary penalties associated with Article 201 and broadens the scope of what constitutes an offense under its provisions. Specifically, it revises the penalty to *prisión mayor* or a fine ranging from ₱20,000 to ₱200,000, or both. This amendment modifies the previous change by substantially increasing the monetary fines and further delineating the categories of prohibited acts, particularly concerning obscene literature and indecent exhibitions.

### 3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT

*   **Elements of the Crime**: RA 10951 substantially modifies and expands the existing elements of the offenses under Article 201.
    *   **Broader Definition of Obscene Literature and Indecent Shows**: The amendment explicitly includes categories of content such as that which "glorifies criminals or condones crimes," "serves no other purpose but to satisfy the market for violence, lust or pornography," "offends any race or religion," "tends to abet traffic in and use of prohibited drugs," and "is contrary to law, public orders, morals, and good customs, established policies, lawful orders, decrees and edicts." This significantly widens the net for what can be considered "obscene literature" or "indecent or immoral plays, scenes, acts or shows."
    *   **Inclusion of Owners/Operators**: Under item 2.a, the amendment explicitly includes "the owners/operators of the establishment selling the same" (obscene literature) as punishable individuals, thereby expanding liability beyond just authors and editors.
    *   **Consolidation and Clarification**: The amendment consolidates previous provisions related to indecent exhibitions and obscene publications, presenting them in a more structured and comprehensive manner. Item 3 also appears to consolidate aspects of previous items 3 and 4, focusing on the sale, giving away, or exhibition of "films, prints, engravings, sculpture or literature which are offensive to morals."

*   **Penalty Shift**: The most pronounced shift is in the penalty.
    *   **Imprisonment Upgrade**: The penalty for the offenses is now *prisión mayor* (imprisonment ranging from six years and one day to twelve years), a significant escalation from *prisión correccional* in its minimum period (imprisonment ranging from six months and one day to two years and four months) under the previous law.
    *   **Fine Escalation**: The fine ranges have been dramatically increased. Previously, the fine was between ₱200 to ₱2,000. The new range is from ₱20,000 to ₱200,000. This represents a tenfold increase in the minimum and a hundredfold increase in the maximum fine.
    *   **Alternative or Conjunctive Penalties**: The law retains the option for the imposition of both imprisonment and fine, as indicated by "or both such imprisonment and fine."

*   **Prescription of Crimes and Bail Eligibility**: While not directly stated as an amendment by RA 10951, the substantial increase in the imposable penalty, particularly the elevation to *prisión mayor*, generally has implications for the prescription of crimes. Offenses punishable by *prisión mayor* have longer prescription periods compared to those punishable by *prisión correccional*. Additionally, bail eligibility for offenses punishable by *prisión mayor* (which can reach up to 12 years) is generally more restricted than for offenses punishable by *prisión correccional*. However, without specific provisions in RA 10951 addressing these aspects, any impact would be a consequence of the increased penalty's classification under existing procedural rules.

### 4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP
The original Article 201 of the Revised Penal Code, enacted in 1930, defined offenses related to public morals through doctrines, publications, and exhibitions. The previous iteration of the law (as presented in the input) already recognized the need to penalize the dissemination of obscenity and doctrines contrary to public morals, albeit with substantially lower pecuniary penalties and a less severe imprisonment term (*prisión correccional* in its minimum period).

Republic Act No. 10951, enacted in 2017, represents a significant modernization and intensification of the State's efforts to combat obscenity and protect public morals. The "Why" behind this amendment is clearly linked to the changing social landscape and the evolution of media and information dissemination, necessitating a stronger deterrent and a more fitting penalty for offenses that were previously met with relatively minor sanctions. The "How" is achieved through a dual approach: firstly, by drastically increasing the monetary penalties, making the financial consequences of such offenses more substantial; and secondly, by elevating the maximum imprisonment term to *prisión mayor*, signaling a more serious view of these transgressions.

Furthermore, RA 10951 refines and expands the definition of what constitutes "obscene" or "immoral" content, reflecting contemporary concerns about violence, drug use, and offensive material targeting specific groups. This amendment does not simply increase penalties; it recalibrates the legal framework to better address the diverse forms of objectionable content prevalent in the current era, moving beyond a more limited, albeit foundational, approach of the original RPC.

The "Why" behind this amendment is clearly linked to the changing social landscape and the evolution of media and information dissemination, necessitating a stronger deterrent and a more fitting penalty for offenses that were previously met with relatively minor sanctions. The "How" is achieved through a dual approach: firstly, by drastically increasing the monetary penalties, making the financial consequences of such offenses more substantial; and secondly, by elevating the maximum imprisonment term to *prisión mayor*, signaling a more serious view of these transgressions.

Furthermore, RA 10951 refines and expands the definition of what constitutes "obscene" or "immoral" content, reflecting contemporary concerns about violence, drug use, and offensive material targeting specific groups. This amendment does not simply increase penalties; it recalibrates the legal framework to better address the diverse forms of objectionable content prevalent in the current era, moving beyond a more limited, albeit foundational, approach of the original RPC.

### ANALYSIS OF ARTICLE 202 OF THE REVISED PENAL CODE AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10951

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Fine Escalation

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
Republic Act No. 10951 substantially increased the monetary fines prescribed for the offense of prostitution under Article 202 of the Revised Penal Code. This amendment modifies the previous change introduced by Republic Act No. 7659 (The Heinous Crimes Law) and subsequent amendments by significantly adjusting the fine amounts to reflect current economic realities, without altering the prescribed penalties of *arresto menor* or *arresto mayor* to *prisión correccional*.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
*   **Elements of the Crime**: This amendment does not alter any of the substantive elements of the crime of prostitution as defined in Article 202. The definition of a prostitute remains the same: "women who, for money or profit, habitually indulge in sexual intercourse or lascivious conduct."
*   **Penalty Shift**: The core change lies in the significant escalation of the monetary fines.
    *   The original fine not exceeding 200 pesos has been increased to not exceeding Twenty thousand pesos (₱20,000).
    *   For recidivism, the fine ranging from 200 to 2,000 pesos has been increased to a range of Twenty thousand pesos (₱20,000) to Two hundred thousand pesos (₱200,000).
    *   The principal penalties of *arresto menor* and the range of *arresto mayor* to *prisión correccional* in its minimum period remain, but the court now has a significantly wider discretion in imposing fines, both as a sole penalty and in conjunction with imprisonment.
*   **Prescription of Crimes and Bail Eligibility**: The increase in fines alone, without a corresponding change in the penalty of imprisonment to a higher grade, generally does not alter the prescription period for the offense. Similarly, bail eligibility would likely remain within the existing framework for offenses punishable by *arresto mayor* to *prisión correccional*. However, the increased fine amounts might indirectly influence the perception of the seriousness of the offense.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
The original Article 202 of the Revised Penal Code (enacted in 1930) provided relatively low fines. The subsequent amendments, particularly Republic Act No. 7659, focused on increasing penalties for heinous crimes, but Article 202 was not directly affected in terms of its imprisonment penalties. Republic Act No. 10951, titled "An Act Adjusting the Penalties for Fines and Forfeitures Provided for in the Revised Penal Code and Other Special Laws," specifically aims to address the erosion of the value of fines due to inflation. Therefore, this amendment is a corrective measure to ensure that the fines imposed under Article 202 retain their deterrent and punitive effect in contemporary economic conditions. It does not introduce new criminal conduct or fundamentally alter the nature of the offense but rather recalibrates the monetary sanctions attached to it, bringing them in line with present-day economic values.

### **ANALYSIS OF AMENDMENT TO RPC ART. 202**

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Decriminalization

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
Republic Act No. 10158 completely overhauls this article by decriminalizing vagrancy as a status offense. It removes the first four paragraphs of the original law, which penalized individuals for lacking apparent means of subsistence, loitering, or being idle. The amendment retitles the article to focus exclusively on prostitution, which is the only act that remains criminalized under this provision.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
-   **Elements of the Crime**:
    -   The crimes of vagrancy defined in paragraphs 1, 2, 3, and 4 of the old article have been abolished. Consequently, the elements corresponding to these acts (e.g., having no means of support, loitering without justifiable purpose, associating with prostitutes) are no longer legally relevant for prosecution under this article.
    -   The amendment retains only the crime of prostitution. The elements remain unchanged: (1) The offender is a woman; (2) who, for money or profit; (3) habitually indulges in sexual intercourse or lascivious conduct.

-   **Penalty Shift**:
    -   There is no penalty shift for the surviving crime of prostitution. The imposable penalty remains *arresto menor* or a fine not exceeding 200 pesos. The enhanced penalty for recidivism also remains unchanged.
    -   The most significant impact is the complete removal of any criminal liability or penalty for the acts formerly constituting vagrancy.

-   **Prescription of Crimes**:
    -   The prescriptive period for the crime of prostitution is unaffected. As it is a light felony punishable by *arresto menor*, the crime continues to prescribe in one (1) year.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
This amendment reflects a significant shift in legislative policy, moving away from the criminalization of poverty and status. The original Article 202 was a classic example of a "status offense," penalizing individuals for their condition (e.g., being poor, unemployed) rather than for a specific injurious act. It was widely criticized as being discriminatory, anti-poor, and a tool for arbitrary arrests against marginalized members of society.

RA 10158, "An Act Decriminalizing Vagrancy," was enacted to align the Revised Penal Code with modern legal and human rights principles that discourage punishing individuals for their social or economic status. By eliminating the first four paragraphs, the law now requires an overt act (prostitution) for criminal liability under this article, rather than merely a state of being (vagrancy). The legislative intent was to address vagrancy as a social welfare concern rather than a criminal one, thereby preventing the justice system from being clogged with cases that primarily stem from poverty.

rpc_codal.content_md:
In addition to the proper administrative action, the penalty of prisión correccional in its minimum period, or a fine ranging from Forty thousand pesos (₱40,000) to Two hundred thousand pesos (₱200,000), or both, shall be imposed upon any attorney-at-law or any person duly authorized to represent and/or assist a party to a case who, by any malicious breach of professional duty or of inexcusable negligence or ignorance, shall prejudice his client, or reveal any of the secrets of the latter learned by him in his professional capacity.

The same penalty shall be imposed upon an attorney-at-law or any person duly authorized to represent and/or assist a party to a case who, having undertaken the defense of a client or having received confidential information from said client in a case, shall undertake the defense of the opposing party in the same case, without the consent of his first client.

amendments.description:
Here is an analysis of the amendment to Article 209 of the Revised Penal Code:

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Fine Escalation | Formal Revision

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
This amendment, Republic Act No. 10951, substantially increases the monetary fine component for the crime of Betrayal of Trust by an Attorney or Solicitor. It also formally revises the wording to include "any person duly authorized to represent and/or assist a party to a case," broadening the scope beyond just "attorney-at-law or solicitor (procurador judicial)". This amendment modifies the previous change introduced by Republic Act No. 7659 by increasing the monetary fine range.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
*   **Elements of the Crime**: The core elements of the crime remain the same: (1) the offender is an attorney-at-law or a person duly authorized to represent and/or assist a party; (2) a malicious breach of professional duty or inexcusable negligence or ignorance; (3) prejudice to the client or revelation of secrets learned in professional capacity; OR (4) undertaking the defense of the opposing party without the consent of the first client after undertaking the defense of a client or receiving confidential information. However, the amendment now explicitly includes "any person duly authorized to represent and/or assist a party to a case," thereby expanding the class of potential offenders beyond licensed attorneys and solicitors, provided they possess the legal authorization to represent or assist a party.

*   **Penalty Shift**: The penalty of *prisión correccional* in its minimum period and/or a fine remains the same in terms of the principal penalty. However, the monetary fine component has been drastically increased. Previously, the fine ranged from 200 to 1,000 pesos. Under RA 10951, this has escalated to a fine ranging from ₱40,000 to ₱200,000. This signifies a significant increase in the financial deterrent and punitive aspect of the offense.

*   **Prescription of Crimes / Bail Eligibility**: While RA 10951 did not alter the penalty classification as a crime punishable by *prisión correccional* in its minimum period, the substantial increase in the fine component may indirectly influence considerations related to restitution or compensation in civil liabilities arising from such betrayal of trust. It does not, however, inherently alter the prescription periods or bail eligibility which are typically tied to the imposable penalty of imprisonment.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
The original Article 209 of the Revised Penal Code (Act No. 3815) established the offense and its penalties. The amendment introduced by Republic Act No. 10951, enacted on August 29, 2017, revises the monetary aspect of the penalty and broadens the definition of the offender. It is crucial to note that RA 10951 serves as a comprehensive adjustment to many fine ranges in the Revised Penal Code, aligning them with inflation and current economic realities. In relation to the original text provided, RA 10951 effectively escalates the monetary penalty while maintaining the imprisonment component and formalizing a wider group of individuals who can commit the offense. The amendment does not restore any older version of the law; rather, it builds upon the existing framework by modernizing the financial penalty and clarifying the scope of persons covered.

TITLE SEVEN
CRIMES COMMITTED BY PUBLIC OFFICERS
rpc_codal.content_md:
Any public officer who shall agree to perform an act constituting a crime, in connection with the performance of his official duties, in consideration of any offer, promise, gift or present received by such officer, personally or through the mediation of another, shall suffer the penalty of prision mayor in its medium and maximum periods and a fine of not less than three times the value of the gift, in addition to the penalty corresponding to the crime agreed upon, if the same shall have been committed.

If the gift was accepted by the officer in consideration of the execution of an act which does not constitute a crime, and the officer executed said act, he shall suffer the same penalty provided in the preceding paragraph; and if said act shall not have been accomplished, the officer shall suffer the penalties of prision correccional in its medium period and a fine of not less than twice the value of such gift.

If the object for which the gift was received or promised was to make the public officer refrain from doing something which it was his official duty to do, he shall suffer the penalties of prision correccional in its maximum period to prision mayor in its minimum period and a fine of not less than three times the value of such gift.

In addition to the penalties provided in the preceding paragraphs, the culprit shall suffer the penalty of special temporary disqualification.

The provisions contained in the preceding paragraphs shall be made applicable to assessors, arbitrators, appraisal and claim commissioners, experts or any other persons performing public duties.

amendments.description:
### **ANALYSIS OF AMENDMENT TO RPC ART. 210 (DIRECT BRIBERY)**

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Penalty Upgrade

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
Batas Pambansa Blg. 871 significantly increases the principal penalties of imprisonment and the corresponding fines for all three modalities of Direct Bribery defined in Article 210. This amendment, being the first in the provided legislative history, represents a substantial upward revision of the original penalties established by the Revised Penal Code. The accessory penalty of special temporary disqualification remains unchanged.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
*   **Elements of the Crime**: This amendment does not alter the essential elements of Direct Bribery. The core requirements—that the offender is a public officer, that they accept an offer or promise or receive a gift, and that such is in consideration of committing a crime, executing an unjust act, or refraining from doing an official duty—remain the same. The amendment is purely penal in nature.

*   **Penalty Shift**: The amendment imposes substantially harsher penalties across all forms of the offense:
    *   **For agreeing to commit a crime (1st par.) and for executing a non-criminal act (2nd par., 1st clause)**: The penalty is elevated by two degrees, from *prision correccional* in its minimum and medium periods (6 months and 1 day to 4 years and 2 months) to *prision mayor* in its medium and maximum periods (8 years and 1 day to 12 years). The fine is also increased from a range based on the gift's value to a fixed floor of "not less than three times the value of the gift."
    *   **For accepting a gift for a non-criminal act not accomplished (2nd par., 2nd clause)**: The penalty is raised by one degree, from *arresto mayor* in its maximum period (4 months and 1 day to 6 months) to *prision correccional* in its medium period (2 years, 4 months, and 1 day to 4 years and 2 months). The floor of the fine is also raised.
    *   **For refraining from an official duty (3rd par.)**: The penalty is elevated by two degrees, from *arresto mayor* in its medium and maximum periods (2 months and 1 day to 6 months) to *prision correccional* in its maximum period to *prision mayor* in its minimum period (4 years, 2 months, and 1 day to 8 years). The fine's floor is similarly increased to "not less than three times the value of such gift."

*   **Prescription of Crimes**: The increased penalties have a direct impact on the statute of limitations. Crimes originally punishable by a correctional penalty (*prision correccional*), which prescribed in ten (10) years, now become punishable by an afflictive penalty (*prision mayor*). Consequently, the prescriptive period for the most severe forms of Direct Bribery is extended to fifteen (15) years under Article 92 of the RPC.

*   **Bail Eligibility**: This is arguably the most significant procedural impact. Under the original law, the penalties were mostly correctional, making bail a matter of right. By increasing the penalty to *prision mayor*, which exceeds six years of imprisonment, the offense now falls under the constitutional provision where bail becomes a matter of discretion, and may be denied if the evidence of guilt is strong.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
This amendment does not revert to a previous version but instead constitutes a sharp escalation from the original framework of the Revised Penal Code. Enacted in 1985, BP 871 reflects a legislative response to the perceived inadequacy of the original penalties in deterring rampant graft and corruption within the public service.

The original RPC, effective in 1932, treated Direct Bribery with penalties that, by modern standards, might be considered lenient. BP 871 represents a significant shift in legislative policy, recategorizing the offense as a much graver crime. By elevating the penalties from the correctional to the afflictive range, the law signals an intent to impose more severe consequences, thereby affecting not only the length of incarceration but also critical procedural matters like bail eligibility and the time within which the state can prosecute the crime. This amendment should be understood as a deliberate effort to strengthen the state's legal arsenal against corruption by making the penalties for bribery more punitive and deterrent.

rpc_codal.content_md:
Any public officer who shall agree to perform an act constituting a crime, in connection with the performance of his official duties, in consideration of any offer, promise, gift or present received by such officer, personally or through the mediation of another, shall suffer the penalty of prision mayor in its medium and maximum periods and a fine of not less than three times the value of the gift, in addition to the penalty corresponding to the crime agreed upon, if the same shall have been committed.

If the gift was accepted by the officer in consideration of the execution of an act which does not constitute a crime, and the officer executed said act, he shall suffer the same penalty provided in the preceding paragraph; and if said act shall not have been accomplished, the officer shall suffer the penalties of prision correccional in its medium period and a fine of not less than twice the value of such gift.

If the object for which the gift was received or promised was to make the public officer refrain from doing something which it was his official duty to do, he shall suffer the penalties of prision correccional in its maximum period to prision mayor in its minimum period and a fine of not less than three times the value of such gift.

In addition to the penalties provided in the preceding paragraphs, the culprit shall suffer the penalty of special temporary disqualification.

The provisions contained in the preceding paragraphs shall be made applicable to assessors, arbitrators, appraisal and claim commissioners, experts or any other persons performing public duties.

### **ANALYSIS OF AMENDMENT TO RPC ART. 210 (DIRECT BRIBERY)**

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Penalty Upgrade

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
Batas Pambansa Blg. 871 significantly increases the principal penalties of imprisonment and the corresponding fines for all three modalities of Direct Bribery defined in Article 210. This amendment, being the first in the provided legislative history, represents a substantial upward revision of the original penalties established by the Revised Penal Code. The accessory penalty of special temporary disqualification remains unchanged.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
*   **Elements of the Crime**: This amendment does not alter the essential elements of Direct Bribery. The core requirements—that the offender is a public officer, that they accept an offer or promise or receive a gift, and that such is in consideration of committing a crime, executing an unjust act, or refraining from doing an official duty—remain the same. The amendment is purely penal in nature.

*   **Penalty Shift**: The amendment imposes substantially harsher penalties across all forms of the offense:
    *   **For agreeing to commit a crime (1st par.) and for executing a non-criminal act (2nd par., 1st clause)**: The penalty is elevated by two degrees, from *prision correccional* in its minimum and medium periods (6 months and 1 day to 4 years and 2 months) to *prision mayor* in its medium and maximum periods (8 years and 1 day to 12 years). The fine is also increased from a range based on the gift's value to a fixed floor of "not less than three times the value of the gift."
    *   **For accepting a gift for a non-criminal act not accomplished (2nd par., 2nd clause)**: The penalty is raised by one degree, from *arresto mayor* in its maximum period (4 months and 1 day to 6 months) to *prision correccional* in its medium period (2 years, 4 months, and 1 day to 4 years and 2 months). The floor of the fine is also raised.
    *   **For refraining from an official duty (3rd par.)**: The penalty is elevated by two degrees, from *arresto mayor* in its medium and maximum periods (2 months and 1 day to 6 months) to *prision correccional* in its maximum period to *prision mayor* in its minimum period (4 years, 2 months, and 1 day to 8 years). The fine's floor is similarly increased to "not less than three times the value of such gift."

*   **Prescription of Crimes**: The increased penalties have a direct impact on the statute of limitations. Crimes originally punishable by a correctional penalty (*prision correccional*), which prescribed in ten (10) years, now become punishable by an afflictive penalty (*prision mayor*). Consequently, the prescriptive period for the most severe forms of Direct Bribery is extended to fifteen (15) years under Article 92 of the RPC.

*   **Bail Eligibility**: This is arguably the most significant procedural impact. Under the original law, the penalties were mostly correctional, making bail a matter of right. By increasing the penalty to *prision mayor*, which exceeds six years of imprisonment, the offense now falls under the constitutional provision where bail becomes a matter of discretion, and may be denied if the evidence of guilt is strong.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
This amendment does not revert to a previous version but instead constitutes a sharp escalation from the original framework of the Revised Penal Code. Enacted in 1985, BP 871 reflects a legislative response to the perceived inadequacy of the original penalties in deterring rampant graft and corruption within the public service.

The original RPC, effective in 1932, treated Direct Bribery with penalties that, by modern standards, might be considered lenient. BP 871 represents a significant shift in legislative policy, recategorizing the offense as a much graver crime. By elevating the penalties from the correctional to the afflictive range, the law signals an intent to impose more severe consequences, thereby affecting not only the length of incarceration but also critical procedural matters like bail eligibility and the time within which the state can prosecute the crime. This amendment should be understood as a deliberate effort to strengthen the state's legal arsenal against corruption by making the penalties for bribery more punitive and deterrent.

### **ANALYSIS OF AMENDMENT TO RPC ART. 211 (INDIRECT BRIBERY)**

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Penalty Upgrade

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
This amendment substantially elevates the principal penalty for Indirect Bribery. The punishment is increased from *arresto mayor* to the significantly graver penalty of *prision correccional* in its medium and maximum periods. The accessory penalties of suspension and public censure are retained alongside the new principal penalty.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
*   **Elements of the Crime**: The amendment introduces no changes to the elements of Indirect Bribery. The actus reus remains the acceptance by a public officer of a gift offered by reason of his office.
*   **Penalty Shift**: This is the core of the amendment, with significant consequences:
    *   **Principal Penalty Duration**: The imposable penalty for the offender is increased from a range of 1 month and 1 day to 6 months (*arresto mayor*) to a much longer term of 2 years, 4 months, and 1 day to 6 years (*prision correccional* in its medium and maximum periods).
    *   **Accessory Penalties**: The nature of the accessory penalties changes due to the higher principal penalty. While under *arresto mayor* the accessory penalty was suspension of the right to hold office and suffrage during the sentence (Art. 44, RPC), the imposition of *prision correccional* now carries the more severe accessory penalties of suspension from public office, the right to follow a profession or calling, and the right of suffrage (Art. 43, RPC).
*   **Prescription of Crime**: The prescriptive period for the filing of a criminal action for Indirect Bribery is doubled. Under the previous law, being punishable by a correctional penalty (*arresto mayor*), the crime would have prescribed in 5 years. With the new penalty of *prision correccional*, the crime now prescribes in 10 years, pursuant to Article 90 of the RPC.
*   **Bail Eligibility**: The crime remains bailable as a matter of right before conviction by the trial court. However, the substantial increase in the penalty makes it a more serious offense, which would typically result in a higher bail amount being fixed by the court.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
This amendment reflects a significant legislative policy shift in treating corruption-related offenses. The original RPC formulation viewed Indirect Bribery as a relatively minor infraction, classifying it on par with less grave felonies punishable only by *arresto mayor*.

Batas Pambansa Blg. 871, by elevating the penalty to *prision correccional*, re-categorizes the offense as a serious breach of public trust. This change demonstrates a clear legislative intent to deter public officers from accepting gifts, even without a specific agreement to perform an act, by imposing a penalty that includes a substantial period of imprisonment. This upward adjustment aligns with a broader state policy of intensifying the legal framework against graft and corruption by ensuring that the punitive consequences are not merely nominal but serve as a genuine deterrent.

rpc_codal.article_title: Frauds Against The Public Treasury And Similar Offenses.
rpc_codal.content_md:
The penalty of prisión correccional in its medium period to prisión mayor in its minimum period, or a fine ranging from Forty thousand pesos (₱40,000) to Two million pesos (₱2,000,000), or both, shall be imposed upon any public officer who:

1. In his official capacity, in dealing with any person with regard to furnishing supplies, the making of contracts, or the adjustment or settlement of accounts relating to public property or funds, shall enter into an agreement with any interested party or speculator or make use of any other scheme, to defraud the Government;

2. Being entrusted with the collection of taxes, licenses, fees and other imposts, shall be guilty of any of the following acts or omissions:

a. Demanding, directly or indirectly, the payment of sums different from or larger than those authorized by law.

b. Failing voluntarily to issue a receipt, as provided by law, for any sum of money collected by him officially.

c. Collecting or receiving, directly or indirectly, by way of payment or otherwise things or objects of a nature different from that provided by law.

When the culprit is an officer or employee of the Bureau of Internal Revenue or the Bureau of Customs, the provisions of the Administrative Code shall be applied.

amendments.description:
Here's an analysis of the changes to Article 213 of the Revised Penal Code based on Republic Act No. 10951, presented from the perspective of a Senior Legal Historian and Bar Exam Subject Matter Expert:

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Fine Escalation

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
Republic Act No. 10951 significantly increased the monetary fine component for the offense of Frauds Against the Public Treasury under Article 213 of the Revised Penal Code. The original penalty was a fine ranging from 200 to 10,000 pesos, which has now been revised to a fine ranging from ₱40,000 to ₱2,000,000. The penalty of imprisonment remains the same: *prisión correccional* in its medium period to *prisión mayor* in its minimum period.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**

*   **Elements of the Crime**: Republic Act No. 10951 does not alter the fundamental elements of the crime of Frauds Against the Public Treasury as defined in Article 213. The offender must still be a public officer, acting in their official capacity, and engaging in schemes or acts that defraud the government in dealings concerning public property or funds, or in the collection of imposts.
*   **Penalty Shift**: The core change lies in the monetary penalty. While the range of imprisonment remains the same, the maximum fine has been drastically increased from ₱10,000 to ₱2,000,000. This signifies a stronger legislative intent to penalize financial malfeasance against the government with more substantial financial consequences. The minimum fine has also been increased from ₱200 to ₱40,000.
*   **Prescription of Crimes and Bail Eligibility**: A substantial increase in the prescribed fine may indirectly impact the prescription of offenses under Article 89 of the Revised Penal Code, depending on the interplay between the imposable penalty and the statutory periods of prescription. However, for offenses punishable by *prisión correccional*, the period of prescription generally remains ten years, regardless of the fine amount. Bail eligibility is generally not directly affected by the fine component unless the fine itself becomes so substantial as to be considered in setting bail amounts, which is discretionary.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
The original text of Article 213, as presented, reflects the penal provisions prior to the significant upward adjustments in fines and penalties for various offenses mandated by later laws. The enactment of Republic Act No. 10951, otherwise known as the "Adjusting the Value of Property and Damage in the Revised Penal Code," aimed to recalibrate the monetary penalties within the Revised Penal Code to account for inflation and the diminished purchasing power of the peso over time.

This amendment *modifies* the previous monetary penalties associated with Article 213 by substantially *increasing* them. It corrects the disparity between the outdated fines stipulated in the original RPC and the current economic realities. The underlying criminal conduct and the imprisonment penalties remain consistent with prior iterations, but the financial sanction has been significantly amplified, reflecting a modernized approach to punishing financial fraud against the state. The "Why" behind this amendment is to ensure that the fines imposed are still meaningful deterrents and reflect the actual financial prejudice caused by such fraudulent acts.
