In all cases in which the law prescribes a single indivisible penalty, it shall be applied by the courts regardless of any mitigating or aggravating circumstances that may have attended the commission of the deed.

In all cases in which the law prescribes a penalty composed of two indivisible penalties, the following rules shall be observed in the application thereof:

1. When in the commission of the deed there is present only one aggravating circumstance, the greater penalty shall be applied.

2. When there are neither mitigating nor aggravating circumstances in the commission of the deed, the lesser penalty shall be applied.

3. When the commission of the act is attended by some mitigating circumstance and there is no aggravating circumstance, the lesser penalty shall be applied.

4. When both mitigating and aggravating circumstances attended the commission of the act, the courts shall reasonably allow them to offset one another in consideration of their number and importance, for the purpose of applying the penalty in accordance with the preceding rules, according to the result of such compensation.

In cases in which the penalties prescribed by law contain three periods, whether it be a single divisible penalty or composed of three different penalties, each one of which forms a period in accordance with the provisions of articles 76 and 77, the courts shall observe for the application of the penalty the following rules, according to whether there are or are not mitigating or aggravating circumstances:

1. When there are neither aggravating nor mitigating circumstances, they shall impose the penalty prescribed by law in its medium period.

2. When only a mitigating circumstance is present in the commission of the act, they shall impose the penalty in its minimum period.

3. When only an aggravating circumstance is present in the commission of the act, they shall impose the penalty in its maximum period.

4. When both mitigating and aggravating circumstances are present, the court shall reasonably offset those of one class against the other according to their relative weight.

5. When there are two or more mitigating circumstances and no aggravating circumstances are present, the court shall impose the penalty next lower to that prescribed by law, in the period that it may deem applicable, according to the number and nature of such circumstances.

6. Whatever may be the number and nature of the aggravating circumstances, the courts shall not impose a greater penalty than that prescribed by law, in its maximum period.

7. Within the limits of each period, the courts shall determine the extent of the penalty according to the number and nature of the aggravating and mitigating circumstances and the greater or lesser extent of the evil produced by the crime.

In cases in which the penalty prescribed by law is not composed of three periods, the courts shall apply the rules contained in the foregoing article, dividing into three equal portions the time included in the penalty prescribed, and forming one period of each of the three portions.

In imposing fines the courts may fix any amount within the limits established by law; in fixing the amount in each case attention shall be given, not only to the mitigating and aggravating circumstances, but more particularly to the wealth or means of the culprit.

When all the conditions required in circumstance number 4 of article 12 of this Code to exempt from criminal liability are not present, the penalty of arresto mayor in its maximum period to prision correccional in its minimum period shall be imposed upon the culprit if he shall have been guilty of a grave felony, and arresto mayor in its minimum and medium periods, if of a less grave felony.

When the offender is a minor under eighteen years and his case is one coming under the provisions of the paragraph next to the last of article 80 of this Code, the following rules shall be observed:

1. Upon a person under fifteen but over nine years of age, who is not exempted from liability by reason of the court having declared that he acted with discernment, a discretionary penalty shall be imposed, but always lower by two degrees at least than that prescribed by law for the crime which he committed.

2. Upon a person over fifteen and under eighteen years of age the penalty next lower than that prescribed by law shall be imposed, but always in the proper period.

A penalty lower by one or two degrees than that prescribed by law shall be imposed if the deed is not wholly excusable by reason of the lack of some of the conditions required to justify the same or to exempt from criminal liability in the several cases mentioned in articles 11 and 12, provided that the majority of such conditions be present. The courts shall impose the penalty in the period which may be deemed proper, in view of the number and nature of the conditions of exemption present or lacking.
Light felonies are punishable only when they have been consummated, with the exception of those committed against persons or property.

When the culprit has to serve two or more penalties, he shall serve them simultaneously if the nature of the penalties will so permit; otherwise, said penalties shall be executed successively, following the order of their respective severity, which shall be determined in accordance with the following scale:

1. Death.

2. Reclusion perpetua.

3. Reclusion temporal.

4. Prision mayor.

5. Prision correctional.

6. Arresto mayor.

7. Arresto menor.

A person sentenced to destierro who is also sentenced to the penalty of prision or arresto shall be required to serve these latter penalties before serving the penalty of destierro.

The fine shall be considered as the last of all the principal penalties listed in the preceding article.

When a fine is so imposed, the duration of the subsidiary liability corresponding thereto, by reason of the insolvency of the offender, shall not exceed that which is provided in rule 2 of article 39.

The civil liabilities of a person found guilty of two or more offenses shall be satisfied by following the chronological order of the dates of the final judgments rendered against him, beginning with the first in order of time.

Whenever the courts shall impose a penalty which, by provision of law, carries with it other penalties, according to the provisions of articles 40, 41, 42, 43, 44, and 45 of this Code, it must be understood that the accessory penalties are also imposed upon the convict.

In cases in which the law prescribes a penalty higher than another given penalty, without specifically designating the name of the former, if such higher penalty should be that of death, the same penalty and the accessory penalties of article 40, shall be considered as the next higher penalty.

Whenever it may be necessary to increase or reduce the penalty of fine by one or more degrees, it shall be increased or reduced, respectively, for each degree, by one-fourth of the maximum amount prescribed by law, without, however, changing the minimum.

The same rules shall be observed with regard to fines that do not consist of a fixed amount, but are made proportional.

The legal period of duration of divisible penalties shall be considered as divided into three parts, forming three periods, the minimum, the medium, and the maximum in the manner shown in the following table:

**TABLE SHOWING THE DURATION OF DIVISIBLE PENALTIES AND THE TIME INCLUDED IN EACH OF THEIR PERIODS**

| PENALTIES | TIME INCLUDED IN THE PENALTY IN ITS ENTIRETY | TIME INCLUDED IN ITS MINIMUM PERIOD | TIME INCLUDED IN ITS MEDIUM PERIOD | TIME INCLUDED IN ITS MAXIMUM PERIOD |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| *Reclusion temporal* | From 12 years and 1 day to 20 years. | From 12 years and 1 day to 14 years and 8 months. | From 14 years, 8 months and 1 day to 17 years and 4 months. | From 17 years, 4 months and 1 day to 20 years. |
| *Prision mayor*, absolute disqualification and special temporary disqualification. | From 6 years and 1 day to 12 years. | From 6 years and 1 day to 8 years. | From 8 years and 1 day to 10 years. | From 10 years and 1 day to 12 years. |
| Prision correccional, suspension and destierro | From 6 months and 1 day to 6 years. | From 6 months and 1 day to 2 years and 4 months. | From 2 years, 4 months and 1 day to 4 years and 2 months. | From 4 years, 2 months and 1 day to 6 years. |
| Arresto mayor | From 1 month and 1 day to 6 months. | From 1 to 2 months. | From 2 months and 1 day to 4 months. | From 4 months and 1 day to 6 months. |
| Arresto menor | From 1 to 30 days. | From 1 to 10 days. | From 11 to 20 days. | From 21 to 30 days. |

In cases in which the law prescribes a penalty composed of three distinct penalties, each one shall form a period; the lightest of them shall be the minimum, the next the medium, and the most severe the maximum period.

Whenever the penalty prescribed does not have one of the forms specially provided for in this book, the periods shall be distributed, applying by analogy the prescribed rules.

No penalty shall be executed except by virtue of a final judgment.

A penalty shall not be executed in any other form than that prescribed by law, nor with any other circumstances or incidents than those expressly authorized thereby.

In addition to the provisions of the law, the special regulations prescribed for the government of the institutions in which the penalties are to be suffered shall be observed with regard to the character of the work to be performed, the time of its performance, and other incidents connected therewith, the relations of the convicts among themselves and other persons, the relief which they may receive, and their diet.

The regulations shall make provision for the separation of the sexes in different institutions, or at least into different departments, and also for the correction and reform of the convicts.

When a convict shall become insane or an imbecile after final sentence has been pronounced, the execution of said sentence shall be suspended only with regard to the personal penalty, the provisions of the second paragraph of circumstance number 1 of article 12 being observed in the corresponding cases.

If at any time the convict shall recover his reason, his sentence shall be executed, unless the penalty shall have prescribed in accordance with the provisions of this Code.

The respective provisions of this section shall also be observed if the insanity or imbecility occurs while the convict is serving his sentence.

Conspiracy and proposal to commit felony are punishable only in the cases in which the law specially provides a penalty therefor.

A conspiracy exists when two or more persons come to an agreement concerning the commission of a felony and decide to commit it.

There is proposal when the person who has decided to commit a felony proposes its execution to some other person or persons.

Article 8. Possession or Use of Prohibited Drugs. - The penalty of reclusion perpetua to death and a fine ranging from five hundred thousand pesos to ten million pesos shall be imposed upon any person who, unless authorized by law, shall possess or use any prohibited drug subject to the provisions of Section 20 hereof.

### **RPC Article Analysis: Article 8**

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Misattributed Provision / Special Penal Law Interaction

*(Note: The provided "New Amendment" text from RA 7659 does not, in fact, amend Article 8 of the Revised Penal Code. It appears to be a provision from a special penal law, likely the Dangerous Drugs Act, which was affected by RA 7659's imposition of the death penalty. The following analysis will proceed by clarifying this error and contrasting the two distinct legal concepts as required for a comprehensive understanding.)*

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
The provided text does not represent a change to Article 8 of the Revised Penal Code. Article 8, which defines the general principles of conspiracy and proposal to commit felonies, has remained substantively untouched since its enactment. The "New Amendment" text is a separate provision from a special penal law concerning the possession or use of prohibited drugs, establishing it as a distinct and severely punished offense. Republic Act No. 7659 (The Heinous Crimes Act) primarily amended various articles of the RPC and provisions of special laws to include the death penalty for certain crimes, including aggravated drug offenses, but it did not rewrite or replace RPC Article 8.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
As there is no direct amendment, the substantive impact is best understood by contrasting the original RPC Article 8 with the special law provision cited.

-   **Elements of the Crime:**
    -   **RPC Article 8 (Conspiracy/Proposal):** The elements remain unchanged. For conspiracy, the elements are: (1) an agreement between two or more persons, (2) concerning the commission of a felony, and (3) a decision to commit it. For proposal, the elements are: (1) a person has decided to commit a felony, and (2) they propose its execution to another person or persons. These are general definitions; they only become punishable when another law specifically penalizes the conspiracy or proposal to commit a specific crime (e.g., conspiracy to commit treason or rebellion).
    -   **"New Amendment" (Drug Possession):** This establishes a *malum prohibitum* offense. The elements are: (1) the accused is in possession of an item identified as a prohibited drug, (2) such possession is not authorized by law, and (3) the accused freely and consciously possessed the said drug. Intent is largely immaterial beyond the consciousness of possession.

-   **Penalty Shift:**
    -   There is no penalty "shift" for Article 8, as it prescribes no penalty itself. The penalty for punishable conspiracies/proposals is dictated by the specific article penalizing it (e.g., Art. 115 for Treason, Art. 136 for Rebellion).
    -   The cited drug provision imposes the harsh, indivisible penalty of *reclusion perpetua* to death, along with a significant fine. This reflects its classification as a heinous crime. This penalty does not apply to the general act of conspiracy under Article 8.

-   **Bail Eligibility:**
    -   The eligibility for bail in cases of conspiracy or proposal depends on the imposable penalty for the specific felony being planned.
    -   Under the cited drug provision, the offense is non-bailable as a matter of right. Given that the imposable penalty includes *reclusion perpetua* and death, bail can be denied if the evidence of guilt is strong, pursuant to the Constitution.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
There is no direct historical or evolutionary relationship between the original Article 8 and the provided "New Amendment" text. They exist in separate legal spheres.

-   **History of RPC Article 8:** This article is a foundational principle of criminal law, defining inchoate offenses. It has been a stable and substantively unchanged part of the Revised Penal Code since 1930. Its purpose is to lay down the general definition of conspiracy and proposal, which the Code and other laws can then reference when penalizing these acts for specific, high-stakes crimes like those against national security.

-   **Context of the "New Amendment":** The text concerning drug possession and its penalty of *reclusion perpetua* to death is a product of the State's escalating "war on drugs." The provision itself originates from special legislation (The Dangerous Drugs Act, R.A. 6425, later superseded by R.A. 9165). The imposition of the death penalty was a specific policy intervention of Republic Act No. 7659 in 1993, which aimed to deter what were considered "heinous crimes." This demonstrates a legislative policy of treating certain drug offenses with maximum severity, entirely separate from the general principles of conspiracy defined in the RPC. The confusion arises because RA 7659 amended many laws, but its spirit—imposing the death penalty—is what is reflected in the provided text, not a direct change to RPC Article 8.

Article 80. Suspension of sentence of minor delinquents. - Whenever a minor of either sex, under eighteen years of age at the date of the commission of a crime, is accused thereof, the court, after hearing the evidence in the proper proceedings, instead of pronouncing judgment of conviction, shall suspend all further proceedings and shall commit such minor to the custody or care of a public or private, benevolent or charitable institution, established under the law for the care, correction or education of orphaned, homeless, defective and delinquent children, or to the custody or care of any other responsible parson in any other place subject to visitation and supervision by the Director of Public Welfare or any of his agents or representatives, if there be any, or otherwise by the superintendent of public schools or his representatives, subject to such conditions as are prescribed hereinbelow until such minor shall have reached his majority or for such less period as the court may deem proper.

The court, in committing said minor as provided above, shall take into consideration the religion of such minor, his parents or next of kin, in order to avoid his commitment to any private institution not under the control and supervision of the religious sect or denomination to which they belong.

The Public Welfare Commissioner or his duly authorized representatives or agents, the superintendent of public schools or his representatives, or the person to whose custody or care the minor has been committed, shall submit to the Court every two months or as often as required, a written report on the good or bad conduct of said minor and the moral and intellectual progress made by him.

The suspension of the proceedings against a minor may be extended or shortened by the court on the recommendation of the Public Welfare Commissioner or his authorized representatives or agents, or the superintendent of public schools or his representatives, according as to whether the conduct of such minor has been good or not and whether he has complied with the conditions imposed upon him. The provisions of the first paragraph of this article shall not, however, be affected by those contained herein.

If the minor has been committed to the custody or care of any of the institutions mentioned in the first paragraph of this article, with the approval of the Public Welfare Commissioner and subject to such conditions as this official in accordance with the law may deem proper to impose, such minor may be allowed to stay elsewhere under the care of a responsible person.

If the minor has behaved properly and has complied with the conditions imposed upon him during his confinement, in accordance with the provisions of this article, he shall be returned to the court in order that the same may order his final release.

In case the minor fails to behave properly or to comply with the regulations of the institution to which he has been committed or with the conditions imposed upon him when he was committed to the care of a responsible person, or in case he should be found incorregible or his continued stay in such institution should be inadvisable, he shall be returned to the court in order that the same may render the judgment corresponding to the crime committed by htm.

The expenses for the maintenance of a minor delinquent confined in the institution to which he has been committed, shall be borne totally or partially by his parents or relatives or those persons liable to support him, if they are able to do so, in the discretion of the court.

### **1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Formal Revision

### **2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
This amendment clarifies two key procedural points and updates an administrative title in the provision for suspension of sentence for minor delinquents. It specifies that the minor's age must be under eighteen at the **time of the commission of the crime**, and clarifies that the judgment being forestalled is a **judgment of conviction**. It also updates the title of the supervising officer from "Public Welfare Commissioner" to "Director of Public Welfare."

### **3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
This amendment, while not altering the elements of any crime, has a significant substantive impact on the application of this special procedural rule for minors.

*   **Age Determination:** The most crucial change is pegging the determination of minority to the "date of the commission of a crime." The original text, which referred to a minor being "accused of a crime," created ambiguity as to whether the age at the time of the act, accusation, or trial should apply. This amendment resolves that ambiguity, ensuring that an offender who was a minor at the time of the act but has turned eighteen by the time of trial can still benefit from the suspension of sentence. This solidifies the law's intent to judge the offender based on their maturity and culpability *at the moment of the offense*.

*   **Procedural Clarification:** By adding the phrase "of conviction" after "judgment," the law clarifies the exact stage at which the court's action takes place. It confirms that the suspension of proceedings occurs *after* a finding of guilt based on the evidence, but *before* a formal judgment of conviction is rendered and entered into the records. This is vital, as it prevents the minor from having a formal conviction on their record, which would carry significant civil and social consequences, thus preserving the rehabilitative aim of the provision.

*   **Administrative Update:** The change from "Public Welfare Commissioner" to "Director of Public Welfare" is a purely administrative update, reflecting a likely reorganization or change in nomenclature within the executive branch. It ensures the article correctly identifies the government official responsible for supervision, but has no substantive effect on the legal rights of the minor.

### **4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
This is the first amendment to Article 80 since its enactment as part of the original Revised Penal Code of 1932. The changes introduced by Act No. 4117 were not a shift in legal philosophy but a necessary refinement to address practical and legal ambiguities that arose from the original text's application.

The amendment was a legislative response to potential inconsistencies in judicial interpretation. By clarifying that the age at the time of the offense is the determining factor, the law prevented disparate outcomes where the speed of the justice system could determine a minor's fate. Similarly, specifying "judgment of conviction" ensured that the procedure was uniformly understood as a post-guilt, pre-conviction remedy, fully aligning the text with the core rehabilitative principle of avoiding the stigma of a criminal conviction for young offenders who are deemed reformable. This amendment, therefore, served to strengthen and clarify the original intent of the law rather than to alter its course.

### **1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Element Modification

### **2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
Republic Act No. 47 significantly narrows the applicability of the suspension of sentence for minor delinquents. The amendment lowers the qualifying age from under eighteen (18) to under sixteen (16) years old and restricts the benefit to cases involving grave or less grave felonies, thereby excluding light felonies.

### **3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
- **Modification of Qualifying Elements:** This amendment does not alter the elements of any specific crime but fundamentally changes the requirements for a minor to qualify for the suspension of sentence under this Article. Previously, any minor under 18 accused of any crime was eligible. Now, eligibility requires the concurrence of two new elements: (1) the minor must be under sixteen (16) years of age at the time of the offense, and (2) the offense charged must be a grave or less grave felony.
- **Penalty Shift:** While not a direct penalty modification, the substantive effect is that certain offenders are now subject to penalties they were previously shielded from. Minors aged sixteen (16) and seventeen (17), as well as any minor under 16 who commits a light felony, are no longer eligible for the suspension of sentence. These individuals will now be subject to a judgment of conviction, though they may still benefit from the privileged mitigating circumstance of minority under Article 68, which can lower the imposable penalty by one or two degrees.

### **4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
This amendment marks a significant departure from the broad protective policy of the original Revised Penal Code. The original Article 80 established a very liberal system, granting courts the discretion to suspend proceedings for any minor under 18, regardless of the crime committed. Republic Act No. 47 reflects a legislative recalibration, introducing a stricter and more qualified approach to juvenile justice within the RPC framework.

By lowering the age to sixteen and excluding light felonies, the law effectively removes a large class of minors (those aged 16 and 17) from the benefit of avoiding a formal conviction. This suggests a legislative intent to hold older minors more accountable, treating them similarly to adults in terms of facing conviction, while still allowing for penalty mitigation. The exclusion of light felonies may have been intended to streamline court processes, avoiding the resource-intensive commitment procedure for minor infractions where a simple penalty might be deemed more efficient.

### **ANALYSIS OF AMENDMENT TO REVISED PENAL CODE ARTICLE 81**

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Administrative Update

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
This amendment retains the original method of executing the death penalty—electrocution—but introduces two significant administrative changes. First, it provides for a future alternative method of execution, gas poisoning, contingent upon the provision of necessary facilities. Second, it imposes a mandatory timeline, requiring that the death sentence be carried out no later than one year after the judgment becomes final.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
- **Elements of the Crime**: This amendment has no effect on the elements of any crime. Article 81 is found in Book One of the Revised Penal Code and governs the procedural and administrative execution of an imposed penalty; it does not define or modify the elements of felonies, which are primarily found in Book Two.

- **Penalty Shift**: There is no shift in the penalty itself. The penalty remains "death." This article exclusively governs the *manner and time* of its execution, not the penalty's classification or duration. The primary impact of Republic Act No. 7659 is felt in other articles of the Code where it upgraded penalties for specific heinous crimes to death, thereby making this administrative article operative once again.

- **Substantive Impact**: The amendment introduces two new substantive procedural standards:
    1.  **Mandatory Timeline**: The imposition of a one-year deadline for execution after a final judgment creates a ministerial duty for the Director of Prisons. This prevents an indefinite stay on death row post-conviction and provides a defined timeframe for the carrying out of the sentence, which was absent in the original text.
    2.  **Alternative Method of Execution**: By providing for gas poisoning as a future method, the law signals a legislative intent to potentially move away from electrocution. This also required a subtle but important change in the text: the right to be anesthetized now applies at the moment of "execution," not just "electrocution," thereby making the right independent of the method used.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
This amendment must be understood within the context of the 1987 Philippine Constitution. The Constitution abolished the death penalty but explicitly granted Congress the power to reinstate it for "compelling reasons involving heinous crimes." Republic Act No. 7659, known as the Heinous Crimes Act of 1993, is the enabling law that exercised this power.

Therefore, the amendment to Article 81 was not an isolated revision but a necessary consequence of the reinstatement of capital punishment. While the original RPC already prescribed electrocution, the provision had been rendered inoperative by the 1987 Constitution. RA 7659 reactivated this provision and expanded upon it.

The relationship to the previous law is one of **reaffirmation and modernization**.
- It **reaffirmed** the core of the original Article 81 by maintaining electrocution as the default method.
- It **modernized and regulated** the process by:
    a) Introducing gas poisoning as an alternative, reflecting a legislative consideration of different execution methods.
    b) Imposing a strict one-year timeline, addressing potential due process concerns related to prolonged stays on death row and ensuring a more systematic implementation of the sentence, a concern not addressed by the original text.

### REPORT ON THE AMENDMENT TO REVISED PENAL CODE ARTICLE 83

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Administrative Update

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
This amendment modifies the rules for suspending the execution of the death penalty and introduces a new procedural step. The suspension period for women is changed from three years post-sentencing to a period covering pregnancy and one year post-delivery. Additionally, it mandates the automatic transmittal of final death penalty case records from the Supreme Court to the Office of the President for clemency review.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
- **Elements of the Crime**: This amendment has no effect on the elements of any crime, as Article 83 governs the procedural execution of a penalty after a final conviction, not the definition or commission of an offense.

- **Penalty Shift**: There is no direct shift in the penalty itself. The amendment alters the *conditions and timing* under which the death penalty may be executed. For women, the suspension is now tied specifically to the physiological and maternal conditions of pregnancy and post-delivery, shortening the previous three-year general reprieve to a more specific one-year period after giving birth. The provision commuting the death sentence to *reclusion perpetua* for convicts over seventy years of age is retained without change. The newly added second paragraph institutionalizes a mandatory review for executive clemency, creating a potential administrative path to avoid execution but not altering the judicially imposed penalty.

- **Prescription of Crimes / Bail Eligibility**: Not applicable. These concepts are irrelevant at the post-final judgment stage of capital punishment.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
This amendment was introduced by Republic Act No. 7659, famously known as the "Heinous Crimes Act," which reinstated the death penalty in the Philippines after its abolition under the 1987 Constitution. The change to Article 83 must be understood within this context.

The previous version of the law provided a broader, three-year suspension of execution for any woman sentenced to death, starting from the date of the sentence. RA 7659 narrows this protection, replacing the fixed three-year period with a more specific one-year suspension post-delivery. While still humanitarian in intent (protecting the mother during pregnancy and the immediate infancy of the child), this change effectively reduces the window during which execution is stayed.

Concurrently, while re-imposing capital punishment, the legislature introduced a new safeguard. The mandate for the Supreme Court to automatically forward the records of every final death sentence to the President creates a non-discretionary, systemic opportunity for the exercise of executive clemency. This reflects a legislative attempt to balance the reintroduction of the death penalty with an added layer of executive review, ensuring that the ultimate power of pardon is proactively considered in every capital case before execution.

### **ANALYSIS OF AMENDMENT TO REVISED PENAL CODE ARTICLE 9**

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Penalty Upgrade

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
Republic Act No. 7659 does not introduce any textual change to Article 9; it re-enacts the provision verbatim. The amendment's substantive effect arises not from altering the language of this article, but from its primary purpose of re-imposing the death penalty for specific heinous crimes, thereby giving renewed operational significance to the term "capital punishment" in the definition of grave felonies.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
This amendment is a quintessential example of a "ghost" law's effect on the Revised Penal Code. While the text of Article 9 remains untouched, its application is profoundly altered.

-   **Elements of the Crime**: This amendment has no effect on the elements of any crime, as Article 9 is purely classificatory, defining felonies based on the penalties imposed.
-   **Penalty Shift**: The crucial impact is on the classification of felonies. Prior to this act, the 1987 Constitution had abolished the death penalty, rendering the phrase "capital punishment" in Article 9 legally inoperative. The highest imposable penalty was *reclusion perpetua*. RA 7659, by re-introducing the death penalty for certain crimes, revitalized this part of the definition. Consequently, felonies designated as "heinous" by RA 7659 and made punishable by death were now definitively classified as capital offenses, the most severe type of grave felony.
-   **Bail Eligibility**: The most significant procedural consequence relates to bail. Under the Constitution and the Rules of Court, an offense punishable by death is non-bailable when the evidence of guilt is strong. By re-classifying certain crimes as capital offenses, RA 7659 automatically rendered them non-bailable under this rule, a direct consequence of the penalty's re-imposition.
-   **Prescription of Crimes**: The prescription period for crimes punishable by death remains at twenty (20) years, the same period applicable to crimes punishable by *reclusion perpetua*. Therefore, this amendment did not alter the prescriptive periods for the affected felonies.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
The evolution of this provision is tied directly to the constitutional status of the death penalty in the Philippines.

-   **Pre-Amendment State (Post-1987 Constitution)**: Following the ratification of the 1987 Constitution, which prohibited the imposition of the death penalty, the term "capital punishment" in Article 9 became dormant. The highest penalty that could be attached to a felony was *reclusion perpetua*, which is an afflictive penalty. Thus, all grave felonies were those punishable by afflictive penalties, with *reclusion perpetua* at the apex.
-   **The "Why" of RA 7659**: Congress enacted RA 7659, known as the Death Penalty Law, in 1993 in response to what was perceived as a rising tide of heinous crimes. The legislative intent was to use capital punishment as a deterrent.
-   **Relationship to Previous Law**: RA 7659 did not reverse or alter the text of Article 9. Instead, it gave new life and legal force to a phrase that had been constitutionally suspended. It did not change the definition of a grave felony but expanded its scope by re-activating its most severe category—capital offenses. This act represents a *revitalization* of a dormant part of the Code's penalty classification framework, rather than a direct textual revision of the article itself.

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Fine Escalation

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
The amendment, Republic Act No. 10951, modifies Article 9 of the Revised Penal Code by increasing the maximum fine imposable for light felonies. Specifically, it raises the limit from Forty thousand pesos (₱40,000) to a new limit of Fifty thousand pesos (₱50,000). This amendment directly modifies the previous text by adjusting the monetary threshold for light felonies.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
*   **Elements of the Crime**: The amendment does not alter the substantive elements defining grave, less grave, or light felonies. The classification of a felony as "light" still hinges on the penalty prescribed by law.
*   **Penalty Shift**: The primary shift is in the monetary component of the penalty for light felonies. Where previously the maximum fine was ₱40,000, it is now ₱50,000. This means that light felonies punishable by arresto menor or a fine not exceeding ₱50,000, or both, fall under this category. This increase in the fine limit could indirectly affect the classification of certain offenses, potentially elevating what might have previously been considered a minor infraction (if the fine was close to the old limit) to a light felony if the prescribed penalty now exceeds the old ₱40,000 limit but remains within the new ₱50,000 limit.
*   **Prescription of Crimes and Bail Eligibility**: The increase in the maximum fine for light felonies could have an indirect effect on prescription periods. Under Article 90 of the Revised Penal Code, offenses punishable by a fine not exceeding ₱40,000 prescribe in five years. With the increase to ₱50,000, light felonies punishable by a fine within this new range would continue to prescribe in five years, as the prescription period is tied to penalties, not specific amounts unless the amount itself defines the penalty category. However, the classification as a "light felony" generally implies less severe penalties, which typically translates to shorter prescription periods compared to less grave or grave felonies. Bail eligibility is generally not significantly impacted by an increase in the maximum fine for light felonies, as these offenses are usually bailable.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
The original Article 9 of the Revised Penal Code defined grave, less grave, and light felonies. The penalty for light felonies was initially defined as arresto menor or a fine not exceeding 200 pesos. Over time, due to inflation and changes in economic conditions, these monetary penalties became disproportionately small and no longer reflected the intent of the law. Republic Act No. 10951, enacted in 2017, serves as a broad revision to several penal provisions, including Article 9, specifically to update these outdated monetary penalties. It addresses the devaluation of the peso by increasing the fine for light felonies from ₱40,000 to ₱50,000. This amendment is a form of **Fine Escalation**, bringing the punitive monetary aspect of light felonies more in line with contemporary economic realities, ensuring that the penalty remains meaningful. This amendment does not revert to an older version; rather, it is an update to the existing structure.

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Fine Escalation

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
This amendment, Republic Act No. 10951, directly modifies the definition of light felonies by significantly increasing the maximum fine that can be imposed. It revises the previous fine of "not exceeding 200 pesos" to "not exceeding Forty thousand pesos (₱40,000)". This amendment modifies the previous change introduced by the original Revised Penal Code by substantially increasing the monetary threshold for light felonies.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
*   **Elements of the Crime**: The amendment does not alter the fundamental elements of any crime classified as a light felony. The core distinction between grave, less grave, and light felonies remains tied to the severity of the prescribed penalty.
*   **Penalty Shift**: The primary impact is on the *maximum fine* that can be imposed for light felonies. Previously capped at a very low amount (₱200), this has been dramatically elevated to ₱40,000. This means that for light felonies punishable by a fine, the courts now have a significantly broader range within which to impose such a penalty.
*   **Prescription of Crimes & Bail Eligibility**: While not directly stated in the text of Article 9, changes to the classification or penalties associated with offenses can have indirect effects. An increase in the potential fine for light felonies does not typically alter the prescription periods of crimes, as these are generally tied to the penalty's maximum duration (e.g., arresto menor vs. arresto mayor). Similarly, bail eligibility is usually determined by the existence of capital offenses or offenses punishable by reclusion perpetua, which are not affected by this fine adjustment for light felonies.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
The original Revised Penal Code (Act No. 3815, enacted in 1930) defined light felonies as those punishable by *arresto menor* or a fine not exceeding 200 pesos, or both. This amendment by RA 10951 (enacted in 2017) reflects a significant economic adjustment. The original fine of ₱200 was established during a period of vastly different economic conditions. The substantial increase to ₱40,000 acknowledges the devaluation of the Philippine peso over nearly a century and aims to restore the punitive and deterrent effect of fines for minor offenses, ensuring that they remain meaningful penalties rather than nominal amounts. This is not a reversion to an older version but rather a modernization of the monetary component of a penalty classification.

Crimes punishable by other afflictive penalties shall prescribe in fifteen years.

Those punishable by a correctional penalty shall prescribe in ten years; with the exception of those punishable by arresto mayor, which shall prescribe in five years.

The crime of libel or other similar offenses shall prescribe in two years.

Light offenses prescribe in two months.

When the penalty fixed by law is a compound one the highest penalty shall be made the basis of the application of the rules contained in the first, second and third paragraphs of this article.

Article 90. Prescription of crimes. Crimes punishable by death, reclusion perpetua or reclusion temporal shall prescribe in twenty years.

Crimes punishable by other afflictive penalties shall prescribe in fifteen years.

Those punishable by a correctional penalty shall prescribe in ten years; with the exception of those punishable by arresto mayor, which shall prescribe in five years.

The crime of libel or other similar offenses shall prescribe in one year.

The offenses of oral defamation and slander by deed shall prescribe in six months.

Light offenses prescribe in two months.

When the penalty fixed by law is a compound one, the highest penalty shall be made the basis of the application of the rules contained in the first, second and third paragraphs of this article.

### **AMENDMENT ANALYSIS: Republic Act No. 4661**

---

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Administrative Update

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
This amendment exclusively modifies the prescriptive period for the crime of libel and other similar offenses. Republic Act No. 4661 reduces the timeframe within which the State can prosecute these crimes from the original two years down to one year. All other provisions of Article 90 remain untouched.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
- **Elements of the Crime**: This amendment has no effect on the elements of libel or any other crime. It is purely procedural in nature, affecting only the time limit for prosecution.
- **Penalty Shift**: There is no change in the penalties prescribed for libel or any other offense. The penalty structure of the Revised Penal Code is not altered by this act.
- **Prescription of Crimes**: This is the core impact of the amendment. The statute of limitations for libel and similar offenses is halved. Consequently, the State's right to prosecute an individual for libel is extinguished one year after the commission of the offense (or its discovery, as the case may be), providing an earlier sense of finality and repose for the accused. This shorter period requires swifter action from the offended party and the prosecution.
- **Bail Eligibility**: Bail eligibility, which is determined by the imposable penalty, is unaffected.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
This amendment represents the first modification to Article 90 since the Revised Penal Code's enactment in 1930. The original text provided a two-year prescriptive period for libel, placing it in a unique category between the six-month period for oral defamation and the five-year period for crimes punishable by *arresto mayor*.

Republic Act No. 4661 adjusted this legislative policy by shortening the period to one year. This change reflects a legislative determination that a two-year window for prosecuting libel was excessively long. By reducing the period, the law balances the State's interest in prosecuting reputational harm with the need to protect individuals from the prolonged threat of criminal charges, encouraging the prompt filing of such actions. This amendment does not revert to a previous state but establishes a new, shorter standard for the prescription of libel.

The period of prescription shall commence to run from the day on which the crime is discovered by the offended party, the authorities or their agents, and shall be interrupted by the filing of the complaint or information, and shall commence to run again when such proceedings terminate without the accused being convicted or acquitted, or are unjustifiably stopped for any reason not imputable to him.

The term of prescription shall not run when the offender is absent from the Philippine Archipelago.

The period of prescription of penalties shall commence to run from the date when the culprit should evade the service of his sentence, and it shall be interrupted if the defendant should give himself up, be captured, should go to some foreign country with which this Government has no extradition treaty, or should commit another crime before the expiration of the period of prescription.

Criminal liability is extinguished partially:

1. By conditional pardon;

2. By commutation of the sentence; and

3. For good conduct allowances which the culprit may earn while he is serving his sentence.

Article 94. Partial extinction of criminal liability. - Criminal liability is extinguished partially:

1. By conditional pardon;

2. By commutation of the sentence; and

3. For good conduct allowances which the culprit may earn while he is undergoing preventive imprisonment or serving his sentence.

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Administrative Update

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
This amendment expands the application of good conduct time allowances (GCTA) as a means of partially extinguishing criminal liability. It now allows an accused person to earn GCTA not only while serving a sentence post-conviction but also during the period they are held under preventive imprisonment prior to final judgment.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
- **Elements of the Crime**: This amendment has no effect on the elements of any crime, as it pertains to the post-offense stage of serving a sentence or undergoing detention.
- **Penalty Shift**: While not altering the imposable penalty for any offense, this amendment has a significant impact on the actual time served. By allowing GCTA to accrue during preventive imprisonment, it effectively shortens the total period of incarceration for qualified individuals, as the time credits earned before conviction are now counted towards the partial extinction of the eventual sentence.
- **Prescription of Crimes / Bail Eligibility**: This amendment has no direct impact on the prescription of crimes or on the eligibility for bail.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
Prior to Republic Act No. 10592, the law was restrictive, granting the benefit of good conduct allowances only to those who were already convicted and serving their final sentence. This created a legal gap where the good behavior of a detention prisoner during the often-lengthy period of trial and appeal went unrecognized for the purpose of GCTA, even though the period of preventive imprisonment itself was credited towards the service of the sentence under Article 29 of the RPC.

The amendment rectifies this inequity by extending the benefit to persons under preventive imprisonment. The legislative intent was to adopt a more rehabilitative and consistent approach, incentivizing good behavior from the moment a person is deprived of liberty, not just after a final judgment is rendered. This change aligns the policy on GCTA with the existing principle of crediting preventive imprisonment, ensuring that an accused person who exhibits good conduct throughout their detention receives the full benefit of the law, thereby facilitating a potentially earlier release.

### **ANALYSIS OF AMENDMENTS TO REVISED PENAL CODE ARTICLE 97**

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Administrative Update

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
Republic Act No. 10592 substantially revises the scheme for Good Conduct Time Allowance (GCTA) by significantly increasing the number of days that can be deducted from a sentence for good behavior. The amendment also expands the scope of the allowance to include persons under preventive imprisonment and introduces an entirely new credit—a special time allowance for studying, teaching, or mentoring.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
*   **Elements of the Crime:** This amendment has no effect on the elements of any crime. It is a post-conviction (and now also pre-conviction) mechanism that deals with the administration and service of sentences, not the definition or commission of criminal offenses.

*   **Penalty Shift:** While the amendment does not alter the *imposable penalties* prescribed by the Code for specific felonies (e.g., *Prision Mayor* remains the penalty for a given crime), it has a profound substantive impact on the *actual time served* by a person deprived of liberty (PDL). The increase in monthly deductions is substantial:
    *   Years 1-2: from 5 days to **20 days**
    *   Years 3-5: from 8 days to **23 days**
    *   Years 6-10: from 10 days to **25 days**
    *   Years 11+: from 15 days to **30 days**
    This creates a much faster path to release for qualified PDLs. Furthermore, the creation of an additional 15-day credit for study, teaching, or mentoring (TTA) can, in effect, double the GCTA for some PDLs, further accelerating their release.

*   **Operational Impact and Substantive Rights:**
    *   **Expansion of Beneficiaries:** The most significant change is the expansion of GCTA's coverage from only "convicted prisoners" to include any offender qualified for credit for preventive imprisonment under Article 29. This recognizes that good behavior during pre-conviction detention should also be rewarded, treating this period as part of the total time served. It effectively makes GCTA a substantive right that accrues from the moment of detention.
    *   **Effect of Appeal:** The law now explicitly states that an appeal does not deprive the accused of GCTA. This secures the right to appeal without the chilling effect of losing potential sentence reductions.
    *   **Retroactivity:** Although not stated in the text, the Supreme Court in *Inmates of the New Bilibid Prison, et al. v. De Lima* (G.R. No. 212719, June 25, 2019) ruled that because RA 10592 is a penal law favorable to the accused, its provisions on GCTA must be applied retroactively. This operational interpretation by the Court had a massive substantive impact, making thousands of PDLs convicted before the law's passage eligible for its benefits.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
This amendment represents a significant evolution in Philippine penal philosophy, moving from a purely retributive model to one that emphasizes restorative justice and rehabilitation.

*   **From Conservative to Liberal:** The original Article 97, a relic of the 1930 Code, provided for minimal sentence reductions. RA 10592 drastically liberalizes this scheme. The "Why" behind this change is twofold: first, to provide a stronger incentive for PDLs to engage in rehabilitative activities and maintain good order within penal facilities; and second, as a practical measure to address chronic and severe jail and prison overcrowding.

*   **Harmonization with Article 29:** By extending GCTA to those under preventive imprisonment, the amendment harmonizes Article 97 with the principles of Article 29, which already credits pre-conviction detention time. It rectifies an inequity where two individuals, one who posts bail and one who does not, would have different starting points for earning GCTA under the old law, despite both eventually being convicted.

*   **Incentivizing Rehabilitation:** The introduction of the special time allowance for studying, teaching, or mentoring is a novel feature. It signals a legislative policy that values active rehabilitation over passive good behavior. It incentivizes PDLs not just to avoid misconduct, but to actively improve themselves and contribute positively to the prison community, furthering the correctional goals of the penal system.

article_versions.content: A deduction of one-fifth of the period of his sentence shall be granted to any prisoner who, having evaded the service of his sentence under the circumstances mentioned in article 158 of this Code, gives himself up to the authorities within 48 hours following the issuance of a proclamation announcing the passing away of the calamity or catastrophe referred to in said article.

Article 98. Special time allowance for loyalty. - A deduction of one fifth of the period of his sentence shall be granted to any prisoner who, having evaded his preventive imprisonment or the service of his sentence under the circumstances mentioned in Article 158 of this Code, gives himself up to the authorities within 48 hours following the issuance of a proclamation announcing the passing away of the calamity or catastrophe referred to in said article. A deduction of two-fifths of the period of his sentence shall be granted in case said prisoner chose to stay in the place of his confinement notwithstanding the existence of a calamity or catastrophe enumerated in Article 158 of this Code.

This Article shall apply to any prisoner whether undergoing preventive imprisonment or serving sentence.

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Formal Revision

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
This amendment substantially revises the original provision by expanding its scope and creating a new, more generous benefit. It now explicitly includes persons undergoing preventive imprisonment, not just convicted prisoners, and introduces a significantly larger sentence deduction of two-fifths for prisoners who choose to remain in their place of confinement during a calamity, rewarding a higher degree of loyalty.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
- **Modification of Conditions for Availment:** The amendment does not alter a crime but modifies the conditions for earning a special time allowance. It creates two distinct grounds for availing the loyalty allowance:
    1.  **The original ground (retained but expanded):** A deduction of one-fifth (1/5) of the sentence is granted to any prisoner (now including a person under preventive imprisonment) who evades service during a calamity under Article 158 but surrenders within 48 hours of the proclamation ending it. The key change here is the expansion of beneficiaries to include preventive prisoners.
    2.  **The new ground (newly created):** A superior deduction of two-fifths (2/5) of the sentence is granted to a prisoner who demonstrates greater loyalty by choosing *not* to escape and remaining in the penal institution despite the calamity.

- **Effect on Sentence Service:** This is not a penalty shift but a significant modification in the computation of time served. The introduction of the two-fifths deduction creates a powerful incentive for prisoners to maintain order and discipline during emergencies, directly impacting their actual period of incarceration. The law now recognizes and rewards two distinct levels of loyalty with corresponding benefits.

- **Clarification of Scope:** The final paragraph, "This Article shall apply to any prisoner whether undergoing preventive imprisonment or serving sentence," removes any ambiguity from the previous text. It ensures that the benefits of the special time allowance for loyalty are extended equally to those held in detention pending trial and those already convicted by final judgment, rectifying a previous omission in the law.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
This is the first amendment to this provision since the Revised Penal Code was enacted in 1930. The original text only contemplated and rewarded one specific act: the return of a prisoner who had already escaped during a catastrophe. The legislative intent was to encourage the recapture of escapees by incentivizing their voluntary surrender.

Republic Act No. 10592 introduces a more modern and progressive penological principle. It recognizes that a greater act of loyalty and discipline is demonstrated by a prisoner who, despite the opportunity to escape during chaos, chooses to stay and respect the authority of the institution. The law now creates a tiered system of rewards: a significant reward (1/5 deduction) for returning after an escape, and a superior reward (2/5 deduction) for not escaping at all. This shift in policy prioritizes and more highly values the maintenance of institutional order over the mere mitigation of a disruption already caused.

article_versions.content: Whenever lawfully justified the Director of Prisons shall grant allowances for good conduct. Such allowances once granted shall not be revoked.

Article 99. Who grants time allowances. - Whenever lawfully justified, the Director of the Bureau of Corrections, the Chief of the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology and/or the Warden of a provincial, district, municipal or city jail shall grant allowances for good conduct. Such allowances once granted shall not be revoked.

Here is the comprehensive analysis of the amendment to Article 99 of the Revised Penal Code.

***

**1. AMENDMENT CATEGORY**
Administrative Update

**2. DESCRIPTION OF CHANGE**
This amendment expands the authority to grant good conduct time allowances. The power, previously vested solely in the "Director of Prisons," is now explicitly granted to the Director of the Bureau of Corrections, the Chief of the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology, and the Wardens of provincial, district, municipal, or city jails. The provision that such allowances are irrevocable once granted has been retained.

**3. LEGAL EFFECT & SUBSTANTIVE IMPACT**
This article does not define a crime and therefore has no elements to modify, nor does it prescribe a penalty. Its legal effect is primarily administrative and procedural, falling under the rules on the extinction of criminal liability.

The substantive impact lies in the administration and execution of sentences. By decentralizing the authority to grant allowances, the amendment streamlines the process for a broader population of inmates. Previously, a legal ambiguity existed for inmates in local jails (city, municipal, provincial), as the law only mentioned the Director of Prisons, who heads the national penitentiary system. This amendment clarifies that all persons deprived of liberty, regardless of their place of detention (national penitentiary vs. local jail), are under the jurisdiction of an official explicitly authorized to grant these time allowances, ensuring uniform application of the benefit.

**4. HISTORICAL CONTEXT & RELATIONSHIP**
The original text of Article 99, drafted in 1930, reflected the centralized correctional structure of that era, vesting authority only in the "Director of Prisons." Over the decades, the Philippine penal system evolved and was administratively divided. The Bureau of Corrections (BuCor) now manages national penitentiaries for prisoners serving long-term sentences, while the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) and Provincial Governments manage local jails for detainees and those serving shorter sentences.

This amendment, introduced by Republic Act No. 10592, was a crucial modernization of the law. It harmonizes the outdated text of the Revised Penal Code with the existing administrative reality of the country's tripartite correctional system (BuCor, BJMP, and Provincial Jails). The change resolves the legal and operational gap by explicitly empowering the heads of these respective agencies to grant good conduct allowances, thereby legitimizing a practice that was necessary for the proper administration of all correctional facilities in the country.
